Hennepin County by the numbers

Who bills and collects property tax in Hennepin County?

Two county offices split the work. The assessor sets market value and classification, and the treasurer's counter at the Government Center collects the money. Property tax questions go to the tax information line at 612-348-3011, staffed Monday through Friday until half past four, or to taxinfo@hennepin.us.

A Hennepin County parcel sits inside several taxing districts at once, usually the county, a city, a school district and some special districts. The county says more than 70 local governments levy on property here, and the auditor turns each levy and the assessment data into a rate for each district. If you plan to sell, the bill on your statement adds up every one of those pieces.

What does Hennepin County look like for someone selling a house?

Hennepin is the most populous county in Minnesota, with Minneapolis as its seat. The Territorial Legislature created it on March 6, 1852, and the mills at Saint Anthony Falls drove the early growth of the county. By 1970 the suburbs held more people than the cities for the first time, which is why a seller in Hopkins or Maple Grove deals with very different local rules than one in north Minneapolis.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page gives these numbers for the county:

  • 1,284,784 residents in the July 2025 estimate, on 554 square miles of land.
  • 539,493 households in 2020 to 2024, with 62.7% of homes owner occupied.
  • A median owner-occupied home value of $392,900 and median household income of $97,653.
  • 587,984 housing units and 3,491 building permits in 2025.

The county holds 22 school districts, including Minneapolis Public Schools, Edina, Minnetonka, Wayzata, Osseo Area and Anoka-Hennepin, and the district a house sits in is part of its tax bill.

When are Hennepin County property taxes due?

Half is due May 15 and half on October 15. When either date lands on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, the deadline slides to the next working day. Minnesota Statutes 279.01 states the same two installments as payable before May 16 and before October 16 when taxes on a parcel exceed $100.

Late payments carry a penalty. The statute sets 2 percent on homestead property and 4 percent on nonhomestead property the day after the due date, adds the same amount again on the first day of the next month, then 1 percent per month through December. Penalty stops growing at 8 percent for homestead and 12 percent for nonhomestead. Hennepin applies late payments to penalty first and taxes second.

One relief valve exists. An owner may ask the county to abate the penalty on a late payment once every ten years, for one half only, after the full tax is paid and with no older unpaid years on the parcel. The application for second half taxes is due November 30.

How do I pay Hennepin County property tax?

Online payment is open for real property. The county lists e-check, credit or debit card, PayPal and Venmo, and a payment counts as made the day it is submitted. Mobile home and personal property accounts have to use another method.

  • E-check costs nothing and is capped at $50,000 per transaction.
  • Cards, PayPal and Venmo are capped at $25,000 per transaction. Visa debit adds a $2.95 flat fee and other electronic methods add 2.29%, and the county keeps none of it.
  • In person, on the 6th floor of the Government Center at 300 South 6th Street, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Card payments there carry a 2.49% service fee.
  • A drop box on the same floor takes checks payable to Hennepin County Treasurer, weekdays from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.
  • By phone at 1-877-626-0017, or by mail to the Hennepin County Treasurer at A-600 Government Center, Minneapolis, MN 55487-0060, postmarked on or before the due date.

Direct payment withdraws from a bank account on May 15 and October 15. Forms must arrive by April 15 for the first half and September 15 for the second.

How is a Hennepin County value set and how do I appeal it?

The assessor assigns a market value as of January 2 each year and mails valuation notices in March. The county says it physically reviews every property once every five years. The value you see now drives the tax you pay the next year, so a notice that looks too high is worth reading closely.

Appeals start informally. Call the assessor whose number is printed on your notice, or go to an open book meeting if your city holds one. If that does not settle it, the formal route is a letter or appearance before the local board of appeal and equalization, then the county board in mid-June. To appear before the county board, call 612-348-7050 or email countyvalueappeal@hennepin.us by the date on the notice. The other formal path is Minnesota Tax Court, and under Minnesota Statutes 278.01 a district court petition for taxes payable in a given year must be filed by April 30 of that year.

Hennepin County property tax calendar, from the county tax overview and assessment pages
WhenWhat happens
January 2Assessor sets market value and classification
MarchValuation notices and tax statements mailed
April to MayCalls, open book meetings and local boards
May 15First half due
Mid-JuneCounty board of appeal and equalization
October 15Second half due
Mid to late NovemberProposed levies and notices for next year
November 25 and afterTruth-in-taxation meetings

Which Hennepin County cities run their own assessor?

Six cities handle assessment themselves, and an owner there calls the city instead of the county. Everywhere else the county assessor at 612-348-3046 answers the question.

  • Bloomington, 952-563-8722
  • Brooklyn Park, 763-493-8175
  • Eden Prairie, 952-949-8511
  • Minneapolis, 612-673-3000
  • Minnetonka, 952-939-8220
  • St. Louis Park, 952-924-2535

Calling the wrong office wastes the spring window, so check the notice mailed to the property before you dial.

What happens to unpaid property tax when I sell in Hennepin County?

Delinquent tax has to be cleared before the deed can be recorded. Minnesota Statutes 272.12 tells the auditor to check for delinquent taxes when a deed comes in for transfer, and the recorder will not accept the deed without the auditor's note that no delinquent taxes remain. The county's recording checklist repeats that properties with delinquent taxes may not be transferred.

Current-year tax is a separate matter. If you sell only part of a parcel, Statutes 272.121 asks for a treasurer's certification that the current year tax on the whole parcel is paid. On a normal whole-parcel sale, ask your title company how this year's tax gets split between you and the buyer, and get a payoff figure from the county if a half is still open.

Can a homeowner in Hennepin County reduce the tax bill?

Homestead status is the main lever. The county says you may qualify if you have a Social Security or individual taxpayer identification number, own the home in your own name rather than as a business entity, and live in it, or a relative does. A homesteaded property can qualify for a reduced classification rate, a reduced taxable market value and the state property tax refund.

Owners who just bought should check the taxpayer name and mailing address on the county property map and send a change form if either is wrong. The Property Watch email service tells an owner whenever a document is recorded against the parcel, which is useful when a payoff or release from an old loan is supposed to be recorded.

More questions about Hennepin County, MN Property Tax Guide

What are the Hennepin County property tax due dates?

May 15 for the first half and October 15 for the second half, with a Saturday, Sunday or holiday pushing the deadline to the next working day. A mailed check needs a postmark on or before the date.

Can I sell my Hennepin County house if the property taxes are unpaid?

Yes, as long as the delinquent amount is paid first. Minnesota Statutes 272.12 bars the deed from being recorded until the auditor confirms there are no delinquent taxes, so the payoff normally comes out of closing.

How do I contest my Hennepin County valuation?

Call the assessor listed on the March notice, then use the local board or the county board of appeal and equalization in spring. For the county board, phone 612-348-7050 or email countyvalueappeal@hennepin.us by the date on the notice.

Does Hennepin County charge a fee to pay by card?

Yes. Visa debit adds a $2.95 flat fee online and other electronic methods add 2.29%, all of which goes to the card processor. E-check online has no fee, and card payments at the counter carry 2.49%.

Who do I call with a Hennepin County property tax question?

Call property tax information at 612-348-3011 or email taxinfo@hennepin.us, Monday to Friday. For value questions, call the assessor at 612-348-3046 unless you live in a city that has its own assessor.

Ramsey County by the numbers

Who handles property tax in Ramsey County?

Most of the county's tax work happens in the Plato Building at 90 Plato Blvd. West in Saint Paul, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Property Tax Services (651-266-2222) mails statements, takes payments and reviews penalty requests. The County Assessor (651-266-2131) estimates value and class. A separate line, 651-266-2002, covers delinquent tax information.

The same building also houses the Recorder, the Examiner of Titles and the tax-forfeited land office, so a seller who needs a payoff and then a recorded deed can finish most errands under one roof. The county's online Property Tax and Value Lookup lets you check taxes and values by parcel.

What makes Ramsey County different from other Minnesota counties?

Ramsey is the state's smallest county and its most densely settled. It measures 170 square miles, of which about 152 are land and 17.8 are water, and the Census Bureau has treated it as completely urbanized since 1990. The seat and largest city is Saint Paul. Seventeen other cities fill out the map, from Roseville, Maplewood and Shoreview to North Oaks, White Bear Lake and Little Canada. Six school districts serve it, including Saint Paul Public Schools, Roseville Area Schools and Mounds View Public Schools.

Interstates 35E, 35W, 94 and 694 cross the county, as do US 10, US 52 and US 61, and the Metro Green Line links Union Depot in Saint Paul with downtown Minneapolis. Alexander Ramsey, first governor of Minnesota Territory, gave the county its name when it was created in 1849.

Here is what Census QuickFacts reports:

  • 541,623 people in mid-2025, down 1.9% from the 2020 base
  • 238,541 housing units, with 60.6% owner-occupied, far below the rural counties
  • A median owner-occupied value of $326,600 and median gross rent of $1,329
  • 221,327 households and a median household income of $81,568
  • 708 building permits in 2025

With nearly four in ten households renting, buyers here read the tax statement closely, and a seller should have it ready.

What did the 2026 assessment show in Ramsey County?

The county's 2026 Assessor's Report says total assessed value of real property rose by $1.4 billion to $78.12 billion, the highest figure in county history. That total absorbed a $66.9 million decline in apartment value. The 2026 values rest on sales that closed during 2025.

Among single-family homes, the sharpest gains in median value came in the Saint Paul neighborhoods of St. Anthony Park and Summit Hill. In the suburbs, North Oaks, Falcon Heights and White Bear Lake led. If your own notice showed a bigger jump than your neighbors', the report gives context, and the Assessor can explain what drove the change on your parcel.

Appraisers walk properties through the year to keep the data consistent. The county says these on-site, in-person inspections follow state requirements.

What notices does Ramsey County mail, and what is coming up?

Every owner gets two mailings per parcel. In mid-March comes the tax statement showing the first and second half for the year, together with the value notice that sets next year's tax. The second mailing, in November, is the proposed tax notice with the amounts being considered for the following year and the dates of budget meetings. Owners who sign up for eNoticesOnline receive them electronically.

For 2027, proposed notices are being delivered between November 11 and 24, so many owners are opening them now. The county's public hearing on its proposed 2027 supplemental budget and levy is Thursday, December 3 at 6 p.m. at the Saint Paul City Hall and Ramsey County Courthouse, 15 W Kellogg Blvd. Comments there are passed to the cities, school districts and other taxing bodies.

How do I dispute a Ramsey County value?

The county asks you to phone the Assessor at 651-266-2131 first, because many questions are settled by phone. Expect a few things on that call:

  • You will not reach an appraiser right away.
  • Staff will ask what your concern is.
  • An appraiser should call you back within three days.

You can mail or email supporting papers such as a recent appraisal or a purchase record. The appraiser will say which format works best. If the phone review does not settle it, the county's appeals page describes open book meetings and formal petitions, and it warns that you must keep paying the tax to avoid automatic dismissal of a petition. Confirm the current year's board dates with the Assessor, since they print on each value notice.

When is Ramsey County property tax due and how steep are the penalties?

Residential property is paid in two installments. The first half is due May 15 and the second half October 15, and a weekend due date moves to the next business day. If a bill totals $100 or less, all of it is due in the spring. Manufactured homes pay August 31 and November 15. Partial payments are taken, and late payments go to penalty first, then to tax. A returned payment costs $30.

2026 Ramsey County penalties on homestead and cabin property, from the county payment page
Payment date passesFirst half unpaidSecond half unpaid
May 162%none yet
July 15%none yet
October 18%none yet
October 168%2%
November 18%4%
December 18%5%
January 2, 202710%7%

Nonhomestead property starts at 4% after May 15 and tops out at 12% before year-end, rising to 14% in January.

Can Ramsey County waive a late penalty?

Yes, once. An owner may request one penalty waiver per parcel every ten years, for either the first or the second half but not both. A first-half request must arrive between May 16 and October 15, and a second-half request between October 16 and December 20. You sign the form and send it with the payment, postmarked or dropped off by the deadline. The county refuses the waiver if the payment bounced, if the parcel has delinquent tax or a payment-plan contract, or if the waiver was used in the last ten years.

Separately, owners can ask the Auditor/Treasurer for an abatement of penalty, interest or costs in cases of exceptional hardship, such as a hospital stay. Call 651-266-2222 to ask. If the county says no, staff will walk through other relief and can set up a partial payment schedule.

What happens if Ramsey County property tax goes unpaid?

Tax turns delinquent on January 1 of the following year. The county then adds interest at 10 percent a year, plus a $25 delinquent fee for publication and notice. Owners have three years to redeem the property before the forfeiture process begins. Notice comes four ways: a courtesy letter in the first week of April, a published list of parcels in a county newspaper for two weeks in May, service of notice by the sheriff, and a certified letter in June.

A Confession of Judgment is the county's formal payment plan. The auditor decides whether it runs five or ten years, a $100 processing fee applies per contract, and interest is 7 percent a year on the unpaid balance. Current tax must be paid on time each year, and an owner can make no more than two such contracts on one parcel. Vacant land is not eligible.

Before listing, ask Delinquent Tax Information at 651-266-2002 for the exact payoff. Minnesota Statutes 272.12 bars a recorder from taking most deeds until the auditor confirms no delinquent tax exists on the land.

More questions about Ramsey County, MN Property Tax Guide

Where is the Ramsey County property tax office?

Property Tax Services is in the Plato Building, 90 Plato Blvd. West, Saint Paul, MN 55107. It is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the phone is 651-266-2222.

Does Ramsey County take partial property tax payments?

Yes. Partial payments are accepted on an installment, with penalty paid off first and then tax. Making them does not stop penalties from growing on the unpaid part, so pay the balance by the due date if you can.

How many years does a Ramsey County owner have to redeem delinquent property?

Three years. Before 2014, homestead, cabin and township property had five years. Notice goes out in April, May and June before forfeiture.

When are Ramsey County's proposed 2027 tax notices arriving?

Between November 11 and 24, 2026. They show the estimated 2027 tax and the meetings where budgets are discussed. The county's own hearing is December 3 at 6 p.m.

Can I ask Ramsey County to forgive a late fee twice?

The standard waiver is once per parcel every ten years. A hardship abatement request is separate and can be made whether or not the waiver was used, but the county grants them mainly for exceptional hardship.

Selling in Dakota County?

Dakota County by the numbers

Who do you call about property tax in Dakota County, Minnesota?

Two county groups split the work. Assessing Services sets value and classification (651-438-4200), and Property Taxation & Records bills, collects and handles delinquent years (651-438-4576). Walk-in service for both is at the Administration Center in Hastings, the county seat, at 1590 Highway 55.

Dakota County is the third most populous county in Minnesota, at about 457,710 people on the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate. The Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers form its northern and eastern edge, and Lakeville is its largest city.

What do sellers face in Dakota County's housing market?

Dakota County mixes dense suburbs in the north with farmland and small towns in the south. Burnsville, Eagan, Apple Valley, Lakeville, Rosemount and Hastings sit among the larger cities, while Farmington, Hampton, Randolph and Miesville keep an older street grid. Wikipedia reports that 54% of residents work outside the county, mostly in the Twin Cities core.

  • School districts include 196 (Rosemount-Apple Valley-Eagan), 191 (Burnsville-Eagan-Savage), 194 (Lakeville), 197 (West St. Paul-Mendota Heights-Eagan), 200 (Hastings) and Special School District 6 (South St. Paul).
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes is $381,000 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median household income is $106,318, and median gross rent is $1,548.
  • Owner-occupied housing is 74.9% of the stock, and 185,931 housing units were counted in July 2025.

A higher home value usually means a bigger property tax bill, so a seller should read the statement before pricing. The county's Tax Estimator page lets you test a number.

When is property tax due in Dakota County?

Real property tax is due May 15 and October 15, and both 2026 dates have passed. Agricultural land and manufactured homes have a November 16 second-half date, which is tomorrow, since November 15 falls on a Sunday this year.

Dakota County property tax due dates by property type (Property Taxation and Records)
Property typeFirst halfSecond half
Real propertyMay 15Oct. 15
Manufactured homeAug. 31Nov. 16
AgriculturalMay 15Nov. 16
Personal propertyMay 15none
Personal property on government-owned landMay 15Oct. 15

A payment mailed to the county must be postmarked on or before the due date or penalties apply. Under Minnesota Statutes section 279.01, homestead tax pays 2% after the due date and non-homestead 4%.

How can you pay Dakota County property tax?

The county lists five ways to pay, and each has its own cost.

  • Online or by phone through Paymentus (1-844-797-9075): cards carry a 2.29% convenience fee, Visa debit a $2.95 fee, and a bank transfer $0.35. Each transaction is capped at $100,000.
  • In person at the Administration Center in Hastings, the Northern Service Center in West St. Paul, or the Western Service Center in Apple Valley, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays, with a 2.49% fee on cards.
  • By mail to Property Taxation & Records, Attn: Taxation, 1590 Highway 55, Hastings, MN 55033-2343.
  • Automatic withdrawal, free, for owners whose lender does not pay the tax and who have no overdue tax. Forms filed now apply to taxes due in 2027, and a cancellation is due 15 days before a due date.

You can look up what you owe in the Property Information Search by entering only your house number.

What happens when Dakota County taxes go unpaid?

Tax unpaid on January 2 becomes delinquent and monthly interest is added. A judgment, which is a tax lien, is entered against the property, owners get a letter in March, and a list of delinquent parcels is published in a local newspaper for two weeks.

The owner then has three years to pay in full or set up a payment plan. If the balance is still open after that, the property forfeits to the State of Minnesota, and the county manages it for the state. For parcels with 2022 or earlier tax unpaid, the sheriff served notice in June 2026 and the pay-or-plan date was August 31, 2026.

Penalty abatement is possible but narrow. The county considers clerical error, hardship such as a death or serious illness, a government-declared emergency, a postal error admitted in writing, and a stop-payment on a lost check made within 30 days. It does not accept a missing statement, a late payment alone, or general financial hardship.

How do you appeal a Dakota County value?

For 2026 values the informal route and the county board are closed. The Special County Board of Appeal and Equalization met June 8, 2026, and after it adjourned Assessing Services could no longer change a 2026 value, so any change now applies to the 2027 assessment for taxes payable in 2028.

A petition to the Minnesota Tax Court is the formal option left. Section 278.01 requires a copy to be served on the county auditor and the petition and proof of service filed with the court administrator by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Dakota County accepts email service at taxpetitions@co.dakota.mn.us, and it advises filing early because the county emails back an acknowledgment that must be filed with the court. Bring recent appraisals or sales of similar homes as evidence, and call the Tax Court at 651-539-3260 with questions.

Which Dakota County relief programs have filing dates?

The county's Home and Property page groups its relief programs together, and its 2026 date list gives a deadline for most of them. Missing one usually means waiting a full year.

  • Homestead, for owners who live in the house, with applications due December 31, 2026.
  • Blind and disabled homestead (Class 1b), due October 1.
  • Green Acres, due May 1, and Agricultural Preserves, due June 1.
  • Senior citizen property tax deferment, disabled veterans, open spaces and property tax exemption, plus state property tax refunds and local option disaster abatement.

The 2026 open book appeal ran March 11 to May 1, and manufactured home homestead applications were due May 29. The county also posts proposed taxes for 2027 on its Home and Property page.

What does the tax do at a Dakota County closing?

The county notes that cities and townships set their own sale rules, especially for wells, septic systems, manufactured homes and owners on Medical Assistance, whose certificate of clearance line is 651-554-6555. Under section 272.12, the county auditor must confirm there is no delinquent tax before a deed is recorded, and Dakota County says it can return a deed for delinquent tax.

Home buyers should also watch the calendar for programs. Homestead applications are due December 31, 2026, and the Blind or Disabled Class 1b applications were due October 1. Open Space applications are due November 3.

More questions about Dakota County, MN Property Tax Guide

What is the next Dakota County property tax deadline?

November 16, 2026, for agricultural property and manufactured homes, since November 15 is a Sunday. Real property was due May 15 and October 15. Homestead applications are due December 31.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Dakota County value?

Only through the Minnesota Tax Court. The county board met on June 8, 2026, so Assessing Services can change only the 2027 assessment. A petition for taxes payable in 2027 is due by April 30, 2027.

How do I pay Dakota County property tax by phone?

Call 1-844-797-9075 and use a Discover, MasterCard or Visa card at 2.29%, a Visa debit at $2.95, or a bank transfer at $0.35. Your payment is complete only once you get a confirmation number.

How long before Dakota County can take a property for unpaid tax?

Owners have three years from the delinquency to pay or set up a payment plan before the property forfeits to the state. Interest builds monthly in that time. Call 651-438-4576 about your parcel.

Does Dakota County give a free way to check my balance?

Yes. The Property Information Search is free, and you enter only your house number to see what you owe. Property Taxation & Records can help at taxation@co.dakota.mn.us or 651-438-4576, and the county also offers a free paperless notice option that sends your statement by email.

Washington County by the numbers

Where can I pay a Washington County property tax bill?

Property Records and Taxpayer Services runs the tax counter at the Government Center, 14949 62nd Street North in Stillwater, with a phone line at 651-430-6175. Mail goes to PO Box 200, Stillwater, MN 55082-0200 and has to be postmarked by the due date. The property tax page adds online payment by e-check (a $0.75 fee) or card (2.35%, with a $1.49 minimum), plus bank bill pay.

Owners in the south or north of the county need not drive to Stillwater, because tax payments are taken at the Government Center and at each service center:

  • Government Center in Stillwater
  • Central Service Center, 1261 Woodlane Drive, Woodbury
  • Cottage Grove Service Center, 13000 Ravine Parkway
  • Headwaters Service Center, 19955 Forest Road North, Forest Lake

The department warns that boxes are emptied the next business day, so a payment dropped after hours on the last day should not be counted on. The same office also takes homestead applications at each of those locations.

How does Washington County differ from its rural neighbors?

Washington County is the metro's eastern edge, bounded by the St. Croix River and Wisconsin. The territorial legislature created it on October 27, 1849, naming it for George Washington, and Stillwater, the seat, calls itself the Birthplace of Minnesota because of an 1848 convention held there. Logging and sawmills came first, with a mill at Marine on St. Croix in 1839. Once the forests were depleted, farming took over, and late in the twentieth century suburban growth from St. Paul added most of today's population.

The county covers 423 square miles, 9.1% of it water, which makes it the fourth smallest in the state by land. It holds 25 cities that lie wholly inside it, with Woodbury the largest, followed by Cottage Grove, Oakdale, Forest Lake and Stillwater. Census QuickFacts reports:

  • 286,895 people in July 2025, up 7.2% since the 2020 base
  • 115,270 housing units, 81.3% owner-occupied
  • A median owner-occupied value of $422,000, with $2,275 in monthly owner costs for homes with a mortgage
  • Median gross rent of $1,710 and median household income of $115,345
  • 2,382 building permits in 2025, and 49.1% of adults holding a bachelor's degree or higher

At those values a one percent shift in assessed value moves the tax bill by a meaningful sum, so the March valuation notice deserves a careful read before any listing decision.

What are the Washington County tax dates and penalties?

Most real estate is split into two equal payments. Agricultural land has its second half on November 15, manufactured homes pay on August 31 and November 15, and personal property is due in full May 15 for most owners. The October 15 deadline for an ordinary house passed a month ago. A proposed-tax notice, the Truth in Taxation notice, is mailed in mid-November, so it is reaching mailboxes now.

Washington County penalty ladder for homestead and cabin property, from the county's published table
If paid on or afterFirst halfSecond half
May 162%none yet
June 14%none yet
August 16%none yet
October 18%none yet
October 168%2%
December 18%5%
January 210%7%

Non-homestead rates run higher, reaching 12% on the first half by October 1. Once January 2 passes, interest starts on unpaid tax, penalties and fees at an annual 8%, rising monthly. A third column in the county table covers owners who skipped both halves.

How does a Washington County appeal work?

Each spring the valuation notice rides in the same envelope as the tax statement, mailed by March 31. For 2026 the county asked owners to call the appraisers at 651-430-6175 first, since many questions end there. An in-person review of the property is required before any adjustment. After that the path depends on where the home sits.

  1. Cities and townships with a local board, such as Hugo (April 3), Forest Lake (April 14) and Lake Elmo (April 15) in 2026, expect you to appear if you want to keep the right to go further.
  2. Other places, including Woodbury, Stillwater, Oakdale and Cottage Grove, used four regional open book sessions in April, where attendance was optional.
  3. The County Board of Appeal and Equalization met June 17, 2026 at 5 p.m. at the Government Center, and an appointment was needed by May 1.
  4. The Minnesota Tax Court takes petitions through April 30 of the year taxes are payable.

A petition has to be served on the county auditor under section 278.01. Washington County prefers its online upload portal, which returns an acknowledgment of service within roughly 5 to 10 minutes. Email and fax are not accepted, and a petition left in the drop box is not service. Owners of income-producing property also owe disclosure documents by August 1.

What happens if Washington County taxes go unpaid?

Tax unpaid after December 31 becomes delinquent on January 2, and the county starts proceedings in the spring with a letter and a published list of delinquent parcels. A $25 fee covers that notice. The first year of delinquency starts a three-year redemption period, and a property that is not redeemed forfeits to the State of Minnesota. The final notice adds a $150 fee and, according to the county, the sheriff delivers a copy to anyone living there.

A Confession of Judgment lets an owner, a lender, a contract for deed buyer or a life estate holder repay over time. The auditor assigns a ten-year plan for residential parcels with 10% down, or a five-year plan for commercial parcels with 20% down. The current year's tax and the yearly installment must both be paid by December 31 to stay in good standing.

Which Washington County relief programs affect a sale?

The homestead market value exclusion was increased beginning with taxes payable in 2025, and it shrinks as value rises. Non-homestead property carries higher penalty rates in the county table, so classification matters when a sale closes close to a deadline.

Two state refunds are described on the county page for owners who live in their property. The standard Property Tax Refund was open to households under $142,490 of 2025 income. The special refund requires a net tax increase of at least 12% and $100, and increases caused by improvements do not count. Forms and instructions are on the Minnesota Department of Revenue website.

How is tax settled when a Washington County house closes?

The county's new homeowner page tells buyers to verify that tax due in the year of sale has been paid, giving the usual May 15 and October 15 halves. Under section 272.12 the auditor certifies delinquent tax before a deed is recorded. Ask the taxpayer services line for a payoff figure during the listing period, and have the title company show the year's split on the closing statement.

More questions about Washington County, MN Property Tax Guide

Can I pay my Washington County taxes in Woodbury instead of Stillwater?

Yes. The Woodbury service center on Woodlane Drive takes tax payments, as do the Cottage Grove and Forest Lake centers. A box payment is collected the next business day, so mail or pay online if the deadline is today.

What interest does Washington County charge on delinquent tax?

Interest runs at an annual rate of 8% on unpaid tax, penalties and fees beginning January 2, increasing monthly. Penalty percentages also step up on that date, so a balance grows quickly.

How do I serve a tax petition on Washington County?

Use the county's online petition portal, which returns an acknowledgment in a few minutes, or hand it to staff at the Government Center counter during business hours. Email and fax service are not agreed to, and the April 30 deadline is strict.

Is there a payment plan for back taxes in Washington County?

Yes, a Confession of Judgment. A residential parcel gets ten years with 10% down, and a commercial parcel gets five years with 20% down. The owner, a lender, a contract for deed buyer or a life estate holder may apply.

When did the Washington County Board of Appeal meet in 2026?

June 17, 2026 at 5 p.m. at the Government Center in Stillwater. Appointments had to be made by May 1 by calling 651-430-6175. Next year's dates appear on the valuation notice mailed in March.

Who to contact in Anoka County

  • Anoka County Property Records & Taxation

Tax rate

Selling in Anoka County?
We buy Anoka County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Anoka County by the numbers

Which Anoka County office sends the tax bill?

Property Records & Taxation does it all under one roof, from valuation to collection. The office is in the Government Center at 2100 3rd Avenue, Anoka, MN 55303. Phone 763-323-5400 for tax questions, or write to proptax@anokacountymn.gov about a valuation. Counter service runs weekdays from opening at eight in the morning until half past four, holidays excepted.

The county's Taxation page adds that Anoka County prints the proposed tax statements for a long list of taxing bodies at once: the county itself, your city, the school district and the state, depending on where the parcel sits and what type of property it is. The bill you pay is a combination of all of those levies.

What is Anoka County like for a home seller?

Anoka County is bordered by Hennepin and Ramsey counties to the south. It has 446 square miles, with the Mississippi River along the southwestern boundary and the Rum River running south through the west. The terrain is low, rolling and wooded, and the lakes include Coon, Ham, Bunker and Centerville.

The county was organized by the Minnesota Territorial Legislature on May 23, 1857, out of parts of Ramsey and Benton counties. Its seat is the city of Anoka, a name from the Dakota word for "on both sides," a reference to the town's place on both banks of the Rum River. Twenty cities fall inside the county, among them Anoka, Blaine, Coon Rapids, Fridley, Columbia Heights, Andover, Ramsey, Lino Lakes and Ham Lake.

Census QuickFacts supplies these numbers:

  • 381,605 people in mid-2025, packed at 862.4 per square mile of land
  • 145,902 housing units, with 80.2% occupied by owners
  • Owned homes valued at a median $346,500 (2020 to 2024)
  • Rent of $1,464 at the median, and owners with a mortgage pay $1,949 monthly
  • 774 building permits in 2025, and a household income median of $101,869

Twenty cities and one township fill the county, and the valuation appeal route depends on which city a house is in.

How does Anoka County value and classify a home?

The assessor values property as of January 2 each year and mails a Notice of Valuation and Classification. The estimated market value on that notice reflects what the assessor thinks the property would sell for on the open market. The class records how the property is used.

On a homestead, the notice also shows a Homestead Market Value Exclusion. The county's explanation gives the formula: a maximum of $38,000 at a market value of $95,000, falling by nine percent of the value above $95,000, and disappearing at $517,200. A seller whose house is worth more than that gets no exclusion, and a buyer in that range will see the full taxable value.

The notice lists other adjustments too, including an exclusion for veterans with disabilities, deferrals under Green Acres, Rural Preserve and Open Space, and a platted vacant land deferral. Taxable market value is the figure after all of those. A separate line shows new improvement value, the assessor's estimate of additions made in the past five years.

Higher value does not automatically raise your bill. The county notes that taxes follow the annual levy and how your value moves compared with neighboring properties.

How do I appeal an Anoka County valuation?

The path depends on your city, and the county's notice page spells it out. Your valuation notice tells you which option applies.

  • In a city that holds its own Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, you must appear there first if you want to go on to the county board.
  • In an Open Book city, you can skip straight to the County Board of Appeal and Equalization in June.
  • Either way, the County Board of Appeal and Equalization is the next stop if the first step did not settle things.

For a first conversation about the number itself, the Taxation page lists proptax@anokacountymn.gov and 763-323-5400. Have your parcel identification number ready.

Beyond the boards, Minnesota Statutes 278.01 lets an owner petition district court or the Tax Court by serving the county auditor, with proof of service filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Statute 274.01 keeps local board meetings between April 1 and May 31.

How can I pay Anoka County property tax?

You can pay four ways, and the county sets out the costs for each. Taxes can be paid at PayAnokaCounty online, by mail, at the Government Center, or through a free automatic direct payment program.

Anoka County payment methods and what each costs (county Payment Options page)
MethodCostNotes
Online card, Apple Pay, Google Pay2.6% feeFee goes to the processor, not the county
Online eCheck$3.50Taken online only
Mail a checkNonePostmark must meet the due date; allow 2 weeks to post
In personNone for cash or check2.6% for cards; drop box available
Direct paymentFreePre-registration required; call 763-323-5400

The county warns that mail is sometimes not postmarked on the day it is dropped off. If the deadline is close, ask the post office counter for a hand-applied postmark, which is free. There is no grace period, and a due date that falls on a weekend moves to the first business day after the weekend. Payment due dates depend on how the property is classified.

When do Anoka County proposed tax statements arrive?

They are mailed in mid-November. The county calls them proposed 2027 property tax statements, and they are not final until the taxing bodies approve their levies in December. The county has posted budget and levy hearing dates on its Taxation page, and eNotices let an owner get the statement by email with the code printed on the proposed notice.

The county names four factors that move a bill: local levies from the city, school district and county, changes in the overall tax base, changes in your assessed value, and how your value change compares with others nearby. Hearings are for budgets, not valuations. The county says the Truth in Taxation meeting is not the place to argue your taxable market value.

The county also reports that in 2026 the legislature created a one-time increase of nearly 15% for homeowners who qualified for the 2025 regular property tax refund, with form M1PR due by August 15, 2027.

Who receives the Anoka County tax statement after I sell?

Often it is still you. Anoka County mails one statement per parcel a year, in mid-March, and a change in recorded ownership after January 1 does not trigger a new mailing. The statement goes to the previous owner or taxpayer, so a buyer and seller should plan for a duplicate request after closing.

A sale, a refinance or a mortgage satisfaction are the usual reasons for a different taxpayer, and each calls for a duplicate. Call 763-323-5400 if you have not received a statement by April 1. Not receiving one does not forgive the penalty or interest.

A manufactured home is taxed on a separate schedule, with statements mailed in July, and its title cannot be transferred until all current and delinquent personal property taxes are paid.

More questions about Anoka County, MN Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay Anoka County property tax in person?

Go to the Government Center in Anoka at 2100 3rd Avenue on a weekday. A service counter and a payment drop box are available. Cash and checks carry no fee, while cards and mobile wallets add 2.6%.

Does Anoka County give a grace period on late taxes?

No. The county states plainly that there is none, and a payment made after either due date draws a penalty that grows the later you pay.

What is the Anoka County assessment date?

January 2 each year. The value notice reflects the assessor's view of what the property would sell for at that time, and the back of the notice lists your appeal options.

Can I appeal my Anoka County valuation at the county board without going to the city first?

Only if your city uses the Open Book format. Where a city holds its own Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, you must appear there before the June county board hearing.

Is the Anoka County proposed tax statement my final bill?

No. The proposed statement shows what you would pay in 2027 if the taxing bodies adopt the budgets they are considering. Levies are approved in December, and the final bill is mailed in mid-March.

Who to contact in Wright County

Selling in Wright County?

Wright County by the numbers

Which Wright County office answers which tax question?

Finance and Taxpayer Services collects the money, and it works from the Government Center at 3650 Braddock Avenue NE, Suite 1400, in Buffalo (main line 763-682-7578). The Assessor, in Suite 1700 of the same building, owns every question about value and class. Walk-in payment runs Monday to Friday, and the county accepts cash, check or card at the counter, with fees on cards and e-checks.

Wright County tax phone lines listed in the county's taxpayer FAQ
TopicNumber
Value and classification763-682-7367 (Assessor)
Special assessments763-682-7573
Ditch assessments763-682-7583
Escrow payments763-684-4540
Mailing address changes763-684-8617
Other tax questions763-682-7584 or 763-682-7572

A drop box stands next to the License Center drive-through on the north side of the building. Online payment is available from the county's taxpayer FAQ. Copies of statements can be printed after you enter the property ID, or by calling 763-682-7577.

Why is Wright County the fastest growing county in Minnesota?

Wright County lies northwest of Minneapolis, bounded on the northeast by the Mississippi River, with rolling land and a great many small lakes. It was organized in 1855 and named for the New York politician Silas Wright. Monticello served first as the seat until 1868, when Buffalo took over. Wikipedia ranks it the tenth largest county in the state and the fastest growing. Otsego, with 19,966 people in 2020, is the largest city, followed by St. Michael, Buffalo and Monticello. Delano, Albertville, Rockford, Annandale, Hanover, Montrose and Cokato round out the larger towns, and Dayton, Hanover and Rockford each reach into Hennepin County.

Census QuickFacts shows how fast things have changed:

  • 157,559 residents in July 2025, up 11.5% from the 2020 count of 141,337
  • 61,161 housing units, with 84.1% occupied by owners
  • $358,900 median value for an owner-occupied home, and $2,098 in monthly costs for those with a mortgage
  • Median household income of $107,209, and 26.3% of residents under 18
  • 1,156 building permits in 2025, and a mean commute of 29.4 minutes

The county added 38.6% to its population in the 2000s and 13.3% in the 2010s, so the assessor is working against a fast-moving market. A seller should compare the valuation notice with recent nearby sales before listing.

When are Wright County property taxes due, and what counts as on time?

According to the county, real estate is paid on May 15 and October 15, agricultural property on May 15 and November 15, manufactured homes on August 31 and November 15, and personal property on May 15 and October 15, though some personal property is due in full in May. When the tax on a parcel is under $100, or under $50 for a manufactured home, the whole amount is due with the first half. The October 15 date has already gone by for houses, while the November date falls on a Sunday this year, so check the stub for the exact day.

The postmark is what counts under state law. The county has warned that many post offices now route mail through a servicing center, so a letter may not be stamped until two or three days after you drop it off. A payment mailed on the last day can therefore be late. Mailing a week early, or paying online, removes the risk.

Statements for real estate are mailed by March 31. Manufactured home statements go out by July 15.

What happens when a Wright County payment is late?

The county applies the penalty on the next business day after the due date, and the amount grows on the first of every month the tax stays unpaid. The chart on the back of your statement shows the figures, and the rates come from state law rather than local choice. Under section 279.01, homestead property starts at 2% and non-homestead at 4%, with the running total capped at 8% and 12%.

Tax left open through the end of the year brings further fees and interest, and the parcel lands on the delinquent tax list. That list matters to a seller, because delinquent tax has to be cleared before the auditor will certify a transfer.

How does a Wright County valuation appeal proceed?

Wright County mails valuation notices each spring, and the assessor's appeals page advises gathering an appraisal, a market analysis or sales data from the right time frame. Then call the Assessor to confirm structure dimensions and condition, and ask for an explanation of how the value and class were set. If you still disagree, work through these stages:

  1. Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, held by some cities and townships in April or early May. Appearing in person or in writing is what preserves your right to go to the county.
  2. Open book meetings in jurisdictions that chose them, where you meet an appraiser and may skip straight to the county board.
  3. County Board of Appeal and Equalization in June. In 2026 it met on Monday, June 15, at 4 p.m. in the Government Center, with appointments required by June 8 so appraisers could inspect first.
  4. Minnesota Tax Court, which you may use directly or after the county board.

The notice itself explains the Homestead Market Value Exclusion, deferrals for programs such as Green Acres and a disabled veterans exclusion. A petition to Tax Court must also meet the April 30 date in section 278.01.

How do ditch assessments affect a Wright County sale?

Wright County keeps a system of official drainage ditches, and owners who benefit pay assessments on top of ordinary tax. The Finance Director acts as the link between those property owners and the County Board, and questions about the charges go to 763-682-7583. A buyer should ask whether the parcel sits on a ditch system and how many annual installments remain.

Special assessments for streets, sewer or similar projects are handled at 763-682-7573. Both kinds appear on the tax statement, so ask the title company to request payoff figures before closing. Under section 272.12 the auditor must certify no delinquent tax before a deed can be recorded.

Who owes the tax when a Wright County house changes hands?

Statements are always addressed to the owner of record as of January 2, which may be the seller well into the year. The county directs people to their settlement statement or to the title company that handled the closing for details on who is responsible. A buyer with a mortgage should confirm with the lender what has been paid from escrow, because a stub reading that taxes were sent to an escrow agent means no payment is due from you.

Property tax refunds belong to the State of Minnesota, and Wright County cannot report on their status. The state number given by the county is 800-652-9094.

More questions about Wright County, MN Property Tax Guide

What is the Wright County property tax payment deadline for 2026?

May 15 and October 15 for ordinary real estate, with agricultural land due in November. The October date has passed. Call 763-682-7584 or 763-682-7572 for a balance and see your stub for the November date.

Does Wright County go by the postmark?

Yes. A payment postmarked by the due date is timely. Because post offices may not stamp mail for two or three days, the county urges people to mail early or pay online.

Who do I call about a Wright County special or ditch assessment?

Special assessments go to 763-682-7573 and ditch assessments to 763-682-7583. Both appear on the tax statement. The Finance Director is the contact point between ditch owners and the County Board.

When did the Wright County Board of Appeal meet in 2026?

Monday, June 15, 2026 at 4 p.m. at 3650 Braddock Avenue NE in Buffalo. Owners had to book by June 8 through the Assessor at 763-682-7367, and a local board or open book meeting comes first.

Why did I not get a Wright County tax statement after buying?

Statements go to the owner of record as of January 2. Look up the parcel online with its property ID or call 763-682-7577, and ask the title company or lender about escrow payments.

Tax rate

Selling in Scott County?
We buy Scott County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Scott County by the numbers

Which Scott County office handles property tax?

Scott County's Property and Taxation Services department covers both ends of the process, from the assessors who set values to the staff who take payments. It sits in the Government Center in Shakopee, the county seat, and answers questions at 952-496-8115 or propertytax@co.scott.mn.us.

The department employs eleven licensed assessors who estimate market value and classification for roughly 58,000 parcels. They also hold the public meetings where owners can discuss a value. Cities and townships in the county, including Prior Lake, Savage, Jordan and Belle Plaine, each add their own levy to the single statement a parcel receives, and so do the school districts and special districts that overlap them.

The county's assessment page carries a short explainer on the move from the homestead market value credit to the homestead market value exclusion, worth a look before you compare two years of statements.

When are Scott County property taxes due?

Scott County bills in two halves, mid-May and mid-October. The payment page set the 2026 second half for Thursday, October 15, which is behind us, so the next deadline is the first half of 2027.

A half that goes unpaid is charged under Minnesota Statutes 279.01: 2 percent for a homestead, 4 percent for any other class, applied again at the start of the next month, with smaller monthly additions of 1 percent after that. Homesteads stop at 8 percent total and other property at 12 percent. One more rule helps late mailers: a county treasurer must forgive the penalty a single time if the postmark is within one business day of the deadline.

That waiver matters more now that the Postal Service dates mail when it first processes it. Scott County recommends that mailers carry the payment to a post office counter and ask for a manual postmark, mail several business days early, or pay electronically.

Ways to pay Scott County property tax (source: Scott County Pay Property Tax page)
MethodWhat to know
Online, e-check$1.50 per transaction
Online, debit or credit card2.3 percent of the amount
MailPostmark must fall on or before the deadline
Outdoor drop boxCircular driveway off Atwood Street, between 4th and 5th Avenue
Curbside drop-offDeadline day only, in the parking lot off 5th Avenue
County librariesDrop box inside the library during the weeks before each due date

What is the best way to pay a Scott County tax bill?

Paying online is the quickest, and it avoids a trip to Shakopee on a busy deadline. The county's online payment center accepts e-check, debit and credit cards, and it does not work with the Internet Explorer browser.

  • If you wait for a receipt at the Government Center on the due date, staff add your name to a standby list, so the county suggests using another route.
  • Mailed payments count as on time only with a postmark dated by the deadline.
  • If your parcel is under a confession of judgment contract, confirm any back-year amounts with taxation staff at 952-496-8115 first.
  • Owners can subscribe to e-notices through the same online payment center and get statements by email.

Whichever route you choose, keep the confirmation for your records.

What does Scott County look like for a homeowner?

Scott County covers 368 square miles in the Minneapolis-St. Paul metro area, which makes it the third smallest Minnesota county by land area. The Minnesota River marks its northern and western boundary. Eight cities share the county: Belle Plaine, Credit River, Elko New Market, Jordan, New Prague (partly in Le Sueur County), Prior Lake, Savage and Shakopee.

Scott County was created by the legislature on March 5, 1853 and honors General Winfield Scott. Farming, lumbering and fur trading along the river drove the early economy. Suburbs later took over: 89,498 people in 2000 became 150,928 in the 2020 census, and the July 2025 estimate stands at 159,017. The Shakopee-Mdewakanton Indian Reservation lies entirely inside the county, within Prior Lake and Shakopee, and Canterbury Park, Valleyfair, Mystic Lake and the Renaissance Festival draw visitors to the county.

The county touches Hennepin to the north, Dakota to the east, Rice to the southeast, Le Sueur to the southwest, Sibley to the west and Carver to the northwest. Work is local as well: the Census Bureau counted 3,655 employer establishments with 60,419 jobs in 2023, up 11.9 percent from the year before, and retail sales of about $2.28 billion in 2022. Residents spend a mean 24.8 minutes getting to work, and 44.1 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

The Census Bureau's latest housing figures show a county of owners:

  • Owner-occupied rate: 83.8 percent, with 54,971 households averaging 2.78 people.
  • Typical owner-occupied home value, 2020 to 2024: $419,400.
  • Monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $2,329. Gross rent: $1,568.
  • Median household income: $119,314.
  • Housing units on July 1, 2025: 59,179, with 883 building permits issued in 2025.

How do I appeal my Scott County valuation?

Begin by gathering evidence that the value is too high, for example an appraisal or the sale price of a similar house nearby. Then call or visit the assessor who covers your city or township.

Next comes the Open Book session or the Local Board of Appeal and Equalization named on your value notice, and either one can lead on to the county board. After that, the Minnesota Tax Court takes petitions filed once the notice is in hand and no later than April 30 of the year the tax comes due.

The county will take service of a petition by email or in a black drop box outside the Government Center, but it ignores anything that arrives after 4:30 p.m. on deadline day. Petitioners still have to file with the district court administrator, and the emailed acknowledgement doubles as proof of service. No reply within 24 hours means you should follow up.

What happens to the tax when a Scott County house sells?

Back taxes remain on the parcel, so a seller who owes earlier years should get the figure from taxation staff before closing. The deed brings state costs of its own: under section 287.21 the deed tax is 0.33 percent of the price for most sales, with a flat $1.65 at $3,000 or below.

Recording also triggers a certificate of value for the county auditor (section 272.115). A buyer cannot get homestead status without it, and a sold house loses its homestead label for the next assessment year until the new owner applies and qualifies. Sellers should ask the closing agent how a half already paid is treated in the settlement figures.

Owners with tax owing, an inherited property or a house that needs repairs sometimes ask for a cash offer, and a buyer can work from the payoff figure the county gives you. Keep the statement and parcel number handy for that call.

More questions about Scott County, MN Property Tax Guide

What is the Scott County property tax phone number?

The department answers at 952-496-8115 and propertytax@co.scott.mn.us.

When was the 2026 second half of Scott County tax due?

Thursday, October 15, 2026, according to the county's payment page. That date is past, so an unpaid balance is already drawing penalty.

What does online payment cost in Scott County?

E-check payments carry $1.50 per transaction and card payments carry 2.3 percent. The county lists fees only for the online route.

A petition to the Minnesota Tax Court, due April 30 of the tax year. Serve a copy on Scott County and file it with the district court administrator.

Who to contact in Stearns County

Tax rate

Stearns County by the numbers

Who handles property tax for a house in Stearns County?

Two county offices share the work. One office sends the statements and takes the money, and the Property Assessment Services group sets each parcel's value and class. The first is the Auditor-Treasurer. Ask the Auditor-Treasurer's office for its current address, phone number and payment mailing address.

The county's property services page groups the tax tools under one heading: the property taxes pages, a Land Management Division that handles property transfers and new tax parcels, a Property Management Portal for business partners, an aggregate tax page and the tax-forfeited property listings. For a seller, the Land Management Division is the office that posts the ownership change on the tax roll after the deed is filed.

The county posts its tax pages in a fixed set: address change for statements, electronic statements, payment options, due dates, penalties, relief options and the senior deferral. Call the Auditor-Treasurer before you list so you know the balance on each half and whether a special assessment is attached to the parcel.

What does the county around St. Cloud look like to a home seller?

Stearns County is the large central Minnesota county built around St. Cloud. It covers 1,390 square miles, with 1,343 of land and 47 of water, and the Mississippi River runs along the northeast edge. The Sauk River drains the middle of the county into the Mississippi at St. Cloud. Wikipedia counts 166 lakes, and the terrain is low rolling hills with savanna soils.

The legislature created the county in 1855. It was meant to be Stevens County, but a clerical error put Charles Thomas Stearns's name on it. German Catholic settlers arrived in large numbers in the 1850s and formed more than twenty parishes, each centered on a small village, and many of those villages are now small cities. The county seat is St. Cloud, and the present courthouse was dedicated in 1922.

Cities other than St. Cloud include Sartell, Waite Park, St. Joseph, Sauk Centre, Melrose, Albany, Paynesville, Cold Spring, Avon and Holdingford, plus a long list of smaller towns and 33 townships. Interstate 94, U.S. 52 and U.S. 71 are the main roads, and St. Cloud Regional Airport lies east-southeast of the city.

How owner-occupied is Stearns County housing?

About 164,000 people live here, and roughly two of every three homes are occupied by their owners. The table draws on Census Bureau QuickFacts, which mixes 2025 estimates with 2020 to 2024 survey averages.

Stearns County: people, homes and money (Census QuickFacts)
MeasureFigure
Population, July 1, 2025164,110
Change since April 20203.7%
Housing units, 202568,027
Owner-occupied rate67.9%
Median owner-occupied value$273,400
Median gross rent$1,068
Median household income$77,066
Building permits, 2025648

A median value of $273,400 is a countywide midpoint, not a price for your street. Rural parcels, lake property and St. Cloud rentals all pull the figure in different directions, so use it only as background.

What is the route for appealing a Stearns County valuation?

Start with the assessment office in spring, then use the local board, then the county board. The county's tax programs menu lists a Local Board of Appeals and Open Book page, and Minnesota Statutes 274.01 sets the local meeting window between April 1 and May 31.

  • Review the valuation notice and compare your estimated market value with recent sales of similar homes nearby.
  • Ask the assessor to look at the value or the classification informally.
  • Appear at your local board of review, or at the open book session if your city or township transferred that duty to the county. Skipping the local step usually closes the county step.
  • If that fails, the county board of appeal and equalization hears the case, and section 274.13 lets it raise or lower a value and change a classification.

Neither board can grant an exemption or take a parcel off the roll. The county's assessment pages also describe the homestead application, the veterans with a disability exclusion and the Green Acres and Rural Preserve programs, so check classification as well as value.

What are the Stearns County tax deadlines and what does lateness cost?

Real estate tax is split into a spring half and a fall half, due May 15 and again October 15, while agricultural land gets until November 15 for the second half. Under Minnesota Statutes 279.01 a late half picks up a 2 percent penalty on homestead property and 4 percent on nonhomestead property, and more accrues each month after that, up to 8 percent for homestead and 12 percent for nonhomestead property.

For 2026 the November 15 date falls on a Sunday. Ask the Auditor-Treasurer which day the county treats as the effective date before you mail a second-half check for farmland. If the envelope is postmarked within one business day of the due date, the treasurer must abate the penalty once, as long as the owner has not used that abatement before.

The county lists five ways to pay: online, payment plans, in person, through an escrow account and by U.S. mail. Counter service runs weekdays, opening at eight in the morning and closing at half past four. The county describes tax-forfeited land as property that goes to the State of Minnesota after three years of nonpayment from the judgment year.

What relief programs and extra taxes appear on Stearns County bills?

The county's tax-related services page names several items that show up on or near a bill. Use this list to ask the right office the right question.

  • Green Acres, Rural Preserve, Class 2c Managed Forest Land and the Sustainable Forest Incentive Act lower the taxable value on qualifying rural land.
  • A residential homestead calculator estimates tax on a single-family home from the municipality, school district and estimated market value.
  • A senior citizen deferral is posted as its own page for owners who struggle with the payment.
  • The county transportation sales tax and wheelage tax fund road projects, and they are county taxes, not part of the property tax line.
  • An aggregate removal tax applies to operators who haul gravel or similar material.

Ask the assessment office which of these apply to your parcel before you set a list price, because a program that ends at sale can change what the buyer pays in the first full year.

Who owes the tax when a Stearns County house changes hands?

The seller owes the tax through the day of closing, and the buyer takes it from there. In Minnesota the first half covers the first part of the year, and the closing agent usually prorates the current year between the parties. Ask the Auditor-Treasurer for the amount due, any special assessment balance and whether any delinquent amount is on the parcel.

The county also tells owners to file an address change if statements should go somewhere new after the sale. Tax liens are recorded in county land records, and the county has a separate page on tax lien recording for state, federal and county liens. If a mortgage escrow pays the bill, the lender still gets a copy and the new owner needs to tell the county where to send the next one.

More questions about Stearns County, MN Property Tax Guide

What is the phone number for the Stearns County Auditor-Treasurer?

Ask the Auditor-Treasurer's office. Its contact details are on the county's property services page.

Where do I mail a Stearns County property tax payment?

Address the check to the Stearns County Auditor-Treasurer, using the payment address printed on your tax statement. Mail it early so the postmark lands by the due date.

Does Stearns County have a homestead tax estimator?

Yes. The county's assessment pages include a residential homestead tax estimator, and the tax-related services page describes a calculator that uses the tax rates for the city and school district you choose along with your estimated market value.

How long before unpaid Stearns County taxes lead to forfeiture?

The county says tax-forfeited land is property that passes to the State of Minnesota after three years of nonpayment from the judgment year. Call the Auditor-Treasurer at once if a balance is delinquent, because the timeline can differ by property class.

Where does a Stearns County owner find the open book appeal information?

On the county's Local Board of Appeals and Open Book page under the property assessment services menu. It sits beside the homestead, exemption and veterans with a disability pages.

Who to contact in Carver County

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Penalty on late payments accrues the day after due date and increases monthly; schedule: first-half 2% May 16, 4% June 1, 5% July 1 ... 8% by Oct 1 (homestead); 4%/8%/9%... for nonhomestead; delinquent Jan 2 adds to 10%/14% (from the county site listing; confirm with the office)

Selling in Carver County?

Carver County by the numbers

Which Carver County offices deal with property tax?

Two Carver County offices share the work, and both sit at 600 East 4th Street in Chaska. Billing and payments go through Property Tax at (952) 361-1910 or custsvc@carvercountymn.gov. Value, classification and homestead questions go to Property Assessment & Homesteading at (952) 361-1960 or assessment@carvercountymn.gov. The building keeps weekday hours of 8:00am to 4:30pm and is closed on government holidays.

The county mails tax statements each year by March 31. A statement that never shows up is no defense against penalty, a point the county's penalty page repeats in bold type.

When are Carver County property taxes due?

On most parcels the first installment falls on May 15 and the second on October 15. Most agricultural property pays its second half on November 15, and manufactured homes pay on August 31 and November 15. State law in Minn. Stat. 279.01 phrases the same dates as payment before May 16 and before October 16.

  • If the statement was not postmarked before April 25, the first-half deadline moves to 21 days past the postmark.
  • A parcel with $100 or less in tax pays the whole amount by the first-half date.
  • Class 4c seasonal recreational property not used commercially takes the homestead penalty schedule.
  • Second-half agricultural property pays no penalty if it is in by November 15.

There is only one statement. The second-half stub is on it, and the county does not mail another in the fall.

What penalty rates apply after a missed Carver County deadline?

Penalty begins the next day and climbs on the first day of every month. The county's schedule runs from 2% to 14%, and the numbers below are for a first-half payment on a residential parcel.

First-half penalty by payment date, Carver County residential property
Paid on or afterHomesteadNon-homestead
May 162%4%
June 14%8%
July 15%9%
August 16%10%
September 17%11%
October 18%12%
January 210%14%

Source: Carver County Penalty Rates page. First-half tax must be paid with its penalty before money counts toward the second half.

  • Only a U.S. Postal Service postmark by the due date counts. Private postage meter marks are rejected.
  • A bank bill-pay check usually carries no postmark, so it must arrive by the due date.
  • Online payments cannot come from a savings account, and a mistyped parcel number can delay a payment into penalty.

Minnesota also gives a one-time break: if a mailed payment is postmarked within one business day after the due date and the owner has not used the break before, the treasurer must abate the penalty (279.01, subd. 2).

How do I contest my Carver County valuation?

Start with a call to the assessor. The county lists four steps: contact the assessment office, attend an open book session or a local board, take the matter to the county board, and finally petition Minnesota Tax Court. You may file with the Tax Court directly at any point.

  1. January 2: every parcel is valued as of this date. The 2026 valuation, used for taxes payable in 2027, rests on sales from October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025.
  2. March: the tax statement and the Notice of Valuation and Classification arrive together.
  3. April and May: local boards meet. State law sets those meetings between April 1 and May 31, and each board must finish within 20 days (Minn. Stat. 274.01). A board may not cut the assessor's total by more than one percent.
  4. June: the county board meets. You can appear only if you attended the local board, and you need an appointment made before June 1.
  5. April 30: Tax Court filing deadline. The 2026 date has passed, so the next one for the 2026 valuation is April 30, 2027.

In November every city, township, school district and the county hold Truth in Taxation meetings. Their notices show this year's tax and an estimate for the following year.

How do I pay Carver County property tax?

The county takes mailed checks, bank bill pay and an online payment system, and its penalty page gives the pitfalls to avoid. A check mailed on the due date needs a U.S. postmark from that day, and a bill-pay payment is on time only if it reaches the county by the due date. Re-enter the parcel number carefully, since a keying error can push a payment past the deadline. The payment portal does not accept a savings account.

Call (952) 361-1910 with questions about what is owed or how penalty is calculated. The county asks that first-half tax be paid in full, with any penalty, before money is applied to the second half.

What changes for property tax when a Carver County house sells?

Check the closing papers for who pays the year's tax, and confirm the full year is paid. The county's public access page shows statement copies and offers email reminders. For a payoff figure on anything past due, call (952) 361-1910.

Homestead status does not travel with the house. A new owner, a move into a trust, a name change or an owner added or removed each requires a new application to the assessor. Under 272.115 the assessor drops the homestead classification for the next assessment year after a sale unless the buyer applies and qualifies, and a buyer cannot be classed homestead if no certificate of value was filed. A qualifying owner may get the homestead market value exclusion, which lowers taxable value.

A seller whose taxes are behind can still sell. Ask the closing agent to request the amount due from the property tax office before the closing date, since penalty rises monthly.

What does Carver County look like for a seller?

Carver County covers 354 square miles of land, which makes it Minnesota's second-smallest county by that measure. Residents numbered 91,042 in 2010 and 106,922 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate stands at 114,379. Chaska serves as seat of government and is the biggest city. Chanhassen lies partly in Hennepin County, so confirm which county bills a Chanhassen parcel before you call.

  • Typical home value (2020 to 2024 Census figure): $453,600
  • Households: 41,175, with 2.65 people each
  • Median household income: $125,946
  • Housing units, July 2025: 44,930

At the median value, each 1% of assessed value is about $4,536, so the March notice is worth reading line by line. The date of your local board meeting is printed on that notice.

More questions about Carver County, MN Property Tax Guide

What is the May deadline in Carver County?

May 15 for most properties. A statement mailed after April 24 pushes that date to 21 days after the postmark. The October installment falls on October 15, or on November 15 for most agricultural land.

Which Carver County number answers valuation questions?

Call the Carver County assessor at (952) 361-1960 or write to assessment@carvercountymn.gov. The assessor can explain the valuation notice and tell you the board dates for your city or township.

Is it too late to challenge the 2026 Carver County value?

The local and county board windows for 2026 and the April 30, 2026 Tax Court deadline have passed. Valuation notices for the next cycle arrive in March, and the next Tax Court filing deadline is April 30, 2027.

What if I mail my Carver County tax payment late?

Penalty begins the next day. If the envelope carries a U.S. postmark within one business day of the deadline and you have never used the abatement before, state law lets the treasurer waive it.

Does the buyer keep my homestead on a Carver County house?

No. The assessor removes the homestead classification for the following assessment year unless the buyer files a homestead application and qualifies. The buyer applies through the assessor's office, and the county treats a new owner, a trust transfer or a name change as an event that needs a fresh application.

Selling in Olmsted County?
