What do Meeker County, MN sellers need to know about property tax?

Three offices in Litchfield split the work. The Auditor builds each bill, the Treasurer collects it, and the Assessor supplies the value and class behind it. All three are inside the Meeker County Government Center at 114 N Holcombe Avenue, which lets a seller finish most errands in a single visit.

State statute sets the dates. Half of the bill is due before May 16 and the other half before October 16, and the Treasurer's page adds that penalty rates also come from state law. Before you list, find out whether the current half is paid and whether anything is open from earlier years.

  • Treasurer, Suite 100: 320-693-5345, with counter service on weekdays.
  • Auditor, Suite 150: 320-693-5212, for parcel ownership records, rates and special assessments.
  • Assessor: 320-693-5205, for homestead filings and value questions.

Where is Meeker County and what are its homes like?

Meeker County sits in west central Minnesota, with Stearns County on its northern edge and McLeod County to the southeast. Its 645 square miles break down as 608 of land and 37 of water. Territorial lawmakers carved it out on February 23, 1856, and honored Bradley B. Meeker, a territorial judge. The county seat moved from Forest City to Litchfield in 1869, after a railroad spur arrived there. Cities include Litchfield, Dassel, Darwin, Cosmos, Cedar Mills, Grove City, Kingston and Watkins, plus part of Eden Valley. Low hills dotted with ponds and lakes cover most of the ground, and Greenleaf Lake State Recreation Area is inside the county.

Meeker County had 23,400 people in the 2020 census and an estimated 23,603 in 2025. That census found 71.9% of residents in rural areas and 12.4% of 10,576 housing units empty. QuickFacts now counts 10,969 units, with 79.3% of occupied homes owned. Owner-occupied homes were valued at $249,000 for 2020 to 2024, households earned $75,446, rent was $904, and only 48 building permits were issued in 2025.

How is a Meeker County tax bill built?

The Auditor's office calculates tax capacity rates and then computes tax on roughly 18,000 parcels covering real property, personal property and mobile homes. Rates follow the budgets of the county, townships, cities, school districts and special taxing districts. Special assessments certified by the county, townships and cities are added to the matching parcel and passed through on the same statement.

Sellers of farmland and rural lots should ask about ditches. The Auditor's office keeps the financial records for each county and joint drainage system and files assessments for their upkeep. After the money comes in, the Treasurer distributes it to the townships, cities, school districts and special districts.

Statements usually mail in late March. Truth in Taxation notices, which estimate the next year's tax, mail in November. Taxes left unpaid for three or more years are subject to forfeiture.

What does a late payment cost in Meeker County?

Minnesota Statutes 279.01 writes the schedule, and it applies the same way here as in every other county. Homesteads get the lower rates and nonhomestead parcels pay twice as much.

Late payment penalty on an unpaid half, from Minnesota Statutes 279.01
WhenHomesteadNonhomestead
Unpaid on the due date2%4%
Still unpaid on the first of the next month2% more4% more
Each later month through December1% more1% more
Ceiling8%12%

If the statement was postmarked after April 25, the first deadline moves to 21 days after the postmark. A bill of $100 or less is payable in one piece on the first date. Farm homesteads and other qualifying agricultural land owe no penalty on the second half if it is paid by November 15. The treasurer may accept an amount different from the installment, and a partial payment is applied to the oldest unpaid installment first.

How can I pay Meeker County property tax?

The Treasurer offers four routes, so choose the one that suits your closing calendar.

  • By mail to the Meeker County Treasurer at 114 N Holcombe Avenue, Suite 100, Litchfield, MN 55355, with a postmark no later than the due date. Owners without escrow find a pre-addressed envelope in the statement mailing.
  • In person at the Government Center with cash, a check or a card. The Treasurer is the first office on the right inside the front doors.
  • By credit card, which adds 2.5% to the total, or by e-check at a flat $1.50 through $10,000 and $10 beyond.
  • By direct debit from checking or savings. Print and mail the authorization form, or call 320-693-5345 and ask for the packet.

Where a mortgage company escrows the tax, the Treasurer sends the figures to that lender, which pays on time.

How do I challenge a Meeker County valuation?

Begin with the assessor and move upward from there. State law lays out three stages, and each limits the next.

First is the local board, which is your town board or city council. It meets in the April 1 to May 31 window and has 20 days to close its work. It can trim single assessments, but its total cuts cannot take more than one percent off the assessor's overall value, and it has no power to grant an exemption. Second is the county board of commissioners and the auditor. It may move a parcel up or down to what it thinks market value is, and an increase requires prior notice and a hearing.

The last stage is a petition to district court or the Tax Court, due by April 30 of the payable year. A late notice resets the clock. An owner first told of a change in value, class or exemption status after February 28 of that year gets 60 days from the mailing date to start the appeal. A board cannot grant an individual reduction to an owner who has refused the assessor access to inspect the property.

How do homestead and refund rules affect a Meeker County sale?

Homestead status sets the penalty rate, and it depends on who lives in the home. Meeker County urges new owners to apply right after moving in. You have to buy and occupy by December 1, and the assessor must receive the form by December 15 for it to count the next year. State law asks for Social Security numbers and signatures from every resident owner and from spouses missing from the deed. Only one homestead is allowed per owner, and an approved one stays in place unless the assessor asks for more proof.

Sellers must report a sale or a change of primary residence to the assessor within 30 days. Miss that window and the property can be taxed at its correct class with a penalty equal to the tax. The state also runs a property tax refund tied to income and tax on a principal residence, and Meeker County directs refund questions to the Department of Revenue.

What should a Meeker County seller check at closing?

Three state rules shape the paperwork. Section 272.12 keeps a deed from being recorded until the auditor has checked for delinquent taxes. Section 272.115 asks for a certificate of value on any sale above $3,000, and the seller, the buyer or an agent can file it. Section 272.121 adds a treasurer's certification for deeds that convey only part of a parcel.

Ask the Auditor about ditch assessments on any rural parcel, and ask the Treasurer for a payoff on the current half. The buyer's lender will want both before funding.

More questions about Meeker County, MN Property Tax Guide

What are the ways to send money to the Meeker County Treasurer?

Walk in, mail a check, use a card or e-check, or sign up for direct debit. The office is at 114 N Holcombe Avenue, Suite 100, Litchfield, and the line is 320-693-5345.

How much is the credit card fee on Meeker County taxes?

A card adds 2.5% of the total. An e-check costs a flat $1.50 up to $10,000 and $10 above.

How steep are late fees on a Meeker County tax half?

A homestead owes 2%, then 2% more the next month, then 1% monthly through December, up to 8%. Nonhomestead owes 4%, then 4% more, then 1% monthly, up to 12%.

What is the Meeker County homestead filing cutoff?

Submit by December 15, and only if you bought and moved in by December 1. That fixes the class for the following year's taxes.

When does unpaid Meeker County tax put a parcel at risk of forfeiture?

The Auditor's office says taxes left unpaid for three or more years are subject to forfeiture. Ask the Treasurer for the payoff amount long before then.

What should a Mille Lacs County, MN seller check first on the tax side?

One combined Property Records and Taxation Office at 635 2nd Street SE in Milaca handles billing here, and the Assessor sits on the ground floor of the same historic courthouse. About 20,000 tax parcels fall under the county. Each real estate transfer goes through that office, where deed tax or mortgage registry tax is collected and the ownership record is changed.

The same office certifies whether taxes are paid, so it is the first stop for a house, cabin or lake lot. Learn which half-year payment is open, whether any older year is delinquent, and which class the parcel carries. Buyers ask about class, since a lakeshore parcel taxed as seasonal recreational is billed on a different basis than a year-round homestead.

  • Property Records and Taxation: 320-983-8310 for general questions, 320-983-8301 about redemption notices, and 320-983-8304 when the online tax database misbehaves.
  • Assessor: 320-983-8311 or assessor@millelacs.mn.gov for value and class questions.

Where is Mille Lacs County and why does the lake matter to a sale?

East central Minnesota is home to Mille Lacs County, named for Mille Lacs Lake (the French words mean thousand lakes). It was formed on May 23, 1857, and spans 682 square miles. About 109 of those, or 16%, are water. The Rum River drains south from the lake, and the county holds Mille Lacs Kathio State Park, Father Hennepin State Park and part of the Mille Lacs Indian Reservation.

Courthouse business happens in Milaca, while Princeton, which extends into Sherburne County, is the biggest city. Isle, Onamia, Foreston, Pease, Bock and Wahkon are the others. Students attend the Isle, Milaca, Ogilvie, Onamia or Princeton school district. The 2025 estimate is 27,753 people, a 4.8% rise over the 2020 base. In 2020 the county had 12,786 housing units and 17.2% stood vacant. Over 2020 to 2024, QuickFacts shows 77.9% of homes owner-occupied, a typical home value of $258,300, household income of $72,729 and a 32.0 minute average commute, the longest among McLeod, Meeker and Mille Lacs.

When is Mille Lacs County property tax due?

Each property type has its own schedule in the county FAQ.

  • Real property: May 15 and October 15.
  • Agricultural property: May 15 and November 15.
  • Mobile homes: August 31 and November 15.
  • Personal property: May 15, with one payment.

Real estate and personal property statements go out in March and must be mailed by March 31. Manufactured home statements follow in the first week of July. Each mortgage company gets its own listing, and escrowed owners still receive a statement for their files. A manufactured home parcel stays in the old owner's name until the certificate of title is transferred, and that transfer first requires every current and delinquent personal property tax to be paid.

How does Mille Lacs County classify cabins, farms and homes?

Class sets the rate applied to your value, and the Assessor publishes short definitions. These stand out for the area:

  • Residential homestead (1a): the primary residence of the owner or a qualifying relative.
  • Residential nonhomestead (4b): a home that is the primary residence of someone else, with no more than three livable units.
  • Seasonal recreational residential (4c): a secondary, weekend or vacation home that is no one's primary residence.
  • Seasonal commercial (4c): resorts and other income property open fewer than 250 days a year.
  • Rural vacant land (2b): unplatted, unimproved land of more than five acres.
  • Managed forest (2c): at least 20 unplatted, unimproved acres with a Forest Stewardship Plan.

A cabin owner whose buyer plans to live there year-round should talk through the change early, since homestead status ends at sale and the buyer must apply. For larger tracts, the Assessor adds that designated public roads are exempt and private roads and driveways are taxable.

What happens when Mille Lacs County taxes go delinquent?

Penalties add up monthly after each due date, yet a tax year is not delinquent until the next January 1. This is the county's sequence for a parcel that stays unpaid.

Mille Lacs County delinquent tax timeline (Mille Lacs County Auditor-Treasurer FAQ)
DateWhat happens
January 1 after the payable yearThe taxes are classified as delinquent and interest begins to accrue monthly
February 15Parcels still owing go on the delinquent list filed with the court administrator, and the owner is mailed a letter
On or before March 20First newspaper publication of the list
At least two weeks laterSecond publication, with paid parcels removed
Second Monday in MayJudgment is taken and the parcel is bid in for the state
Usually three years afterRedemption period ends in most cases

Someone unable to pay in full can sign a confession of judgment. It folds delinquent tax, special assessments, penalties, costs and interest into a single sum paid over 5 or 10 years, depending on class, and the plan is cancelled if current-year tax lapses. Notices of expiration of redemption are the last step before forfeiture. They go out by certified mail, the sheriff serves them, and the county paper prints them.

How can I pay Mille Lacs County property tax?

The online portal finds statements by owner name, parcel ID, street address, or section, township and range. Paying there adds a processor fee: 2.35% on a card, with a $2.00 floor, or $2.00 on an e-check, and the county keeps none of it. Other payments go by mail to the Property Records and Taxation Office, 635 2nd Street SE, Milaca, MN 56353. A declined online payment is a question for your bank. If the database shows an error, try again in 15 minutes and then call 320-983-8304.

How do I appeal a Mille Lacs County valuation?

Your Notice of Valuation and Classification comes in March, at least ten days ahead of the meeting in your township or city. The meeting details are printed at the bottom, and some jurisdictions run open book sessions with the assessor in place of a formal board.

The county suggests gathering proof such as a recent appraisal or comparable sales, having the Assessor review the data, then presenting at the local board in April or May in person, through a representative or by letter. Next comes an appointment with the county board in June, which is open only to owners who made the local appeal first. Anything still unresolved can go to the Minnesota Tax Court, with the petition filed before April 30 of the payable year.

For Tax Court, the county's instructions call for four copies of the petition and five of the tax statement. Serve the Assessor, the County Attorney and the Auditor-Treasurer, then file the original with the court administrator and pay the fee. Expect a trial date within a year.

Which tax breaks and refunds apply to Mille Lacs County owners?

The county's Assessor page says the homestead market value exclusion for taxes payable in 2025 peaked at $38,000 on a $95,000 home and ended for homes worth more than $517,200. It shrinks the taxable value of a homestead and therefore the net tax. Ask the Assessor for current figures.

Minnesota also pays an income-based homestead refund. The county does not handle it and routes questions to the Department of Revenue. A Form M1PR claim has to include a tax statement showing no delinquent tax on the homestead. August 15 is the due date, with late returns accepted until August 15 of the following year, and timely claims are paid in late September or early October. The Assessor is also collecting reassessment questionnaires for 2027, the year each property gets its physical review under the five-year cycle.

What do sellers in Mille Lacs County need to settle before closing?

Request a payoff for the open half and a certification of paid or unpaid tax from the Property Records and Taxation Office. Under Minnesota Statutes 272.12 a deed is not recorded until the auditor confirms no delinquent taxes and enters the transfer. Sales above $3,000 need a certificate of value (272.115), and homestead status drops off after a transfer until the buyer applies and qualifies.

The Assessor sends a sales verification questionnaire for sales in the county. The county uses verified sales to study the market and set values, and the state uses the same studies for refunds and aid payments.

More questions about Mille Lacs County, MN Property Tax Guide

What is the mailing address for a Mille Lacs County tax check?

Send it to the Property Records and Taxation Office, 635 2nd Street SE, Milaca, MN 56353, or pay through the online portal. Call 320-983-8310 with questions.

What are the Mille Lacs County tax due dates?

Real property is due May 15 and October 15, and agricultural property is due May 15 and November 15. Mobile homes are due August 31 and November 15, and personal property is due May 15.

What fees apply when paying Mille Lacs County taxes online?

Cards cost 2.35% with a $2.00 minimum, and e-checks cost $2.00. The processor collects both and the county gets nothing.

Is there an installment plan for back taxes in Mille Lacs County?

Yes. A confession of judgment spreads delinquent taxes, assessments, penalties, costs and interest across 5 or 10 years, provided current-year taxes keep getting paid.

Can I skip the local meeting and go straight to the Mille Lacs County board?

No. The June county meeting is open only after you raise the concern at the local board or open book meeting in April or May. Tax Court petitions are due before April 30.

Who runs property tax in Aitkin County?

Responsibility is split. One office sets the value and class of each parcel, and another sends the bills and takes payment. The Assessor's Office answers at 218-927-7327. The Treasurer is at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119, Aitkin, MN 56431, and takes calls at 218-927-7325.

The Assessor's page says market value and classification are the main inputs to a tax bill, and that the office works under Minnesota statutes, Department of Revenue directives and County Board directives. A free parcel viewer called LINK shows basic parcel data. More detailed building records, including dimensions and sales reports, need a paid subscription, which the Assessor can explain by phone.

A seller here will end up talking to both: the Assessor about value and class, and the Treasurer about any balance on the parcel before the deed is signed.

What does the Aitkin County housing market look like?

Aitkin County sits in east central Minnesota and its seat is the city of Aitkin. Total area is 1,995 square miles, with 174 of them water. The Mississippi River flows south through the west central part, the terrain is wooded rolling hills, and Savanna Portage State Park and Rice Lake National Wildlife Refuge are among the protected areas on the map.

The first version of the county dates to 1857, when it carried the name Aiken, and the current spelling came in 1872. Its namesake, William Alexander Aitken, traded furs for the American Fur Company, and local government was organized in 1871. January lows in the city of Aitkin average about 0 degrees Fahrenheit, with a recorded extreme of minus 47 in 1972.

Census QuickFacts figures worth knowing before you price a house here:

  • Population of 16,252 as of July 2025, about 8.6 people per square mile of land
  • 14,681 housing units, 85.3% lived in by their owners
  • Median value of an owned home: $255,800 (2020 to 2024 survey years)
  • Households earn a median $60,833, and 35.7% of residents are past 65
  • 214 building permits in 2025, plus a 27.7 minute average drive to work

Owners dominate, and the older age profile is worth keeping in mind if the house you are selling belonged to a relative.

Is Aitkin County inspecting properties for 2027?

Yes, in a set of areas. A 2027 reassessment is listed on the Assessor's page, with appraisers on the road since May 2026. An inspection can land anywhere from May 2026 to February 2027, so one may still be ahead.

The areas on the list are Ball Bluff, Balsam, Fleming, Hazelton, Jevne, Macville, Malmo and Turner townships, unorganized territories 51-22, 52-24 and 52-25, and the city of Hill City. The county explains that this is a physical inspection used to check and fix its records, and that state law calls for it on all taxable property at least every five years.

Owners who want to be there for the walk-through can phone 218-927-7327, and the office also asks to hear about any hazards to avoid on the land. Keep receipts for recent repairs handy if you are in one of these areas.

How do I appeal an Aitkin County valuation or classification?

The county's appeals page sets a sequence, and the first step is a phone call:

  • Contact the Assessor's Office and have the front and back of your valuation notice in front of you.
  • Next comes the local board of appeal, staffed by the township board or city council, or an Open Book session if that is what your notice lists. At Open Book, the assessors review the case and decide, and that decision can still go to the county board.
  • After that is the county board, which meets in June. You schedule a time through the County Assessor, and the local step comes first unless your area has no local board.
  • The last stop is the Minnesota Tax Court, which the county says accepts petitions even from owners who skipped the earlier steps. Its deadline is April 30 of the taxes-payable year.

Statute 274.01 puts local board meetings in April and May and caps their combined reductions at one percent of the assessor's total. Under 278.01, an owner may instead serve a petition on the county auditor and file it in district court.

What are the Aitkin County tax due dates?

Bills come in two installments, one in mid-May and one in mid-October. These are the points that matter for an Aitkin County parcel:

Payment rules for Aitkin County parcels (Treasurer FAQ and Statute 279.01)
ItemWhat applies
First halfDue before May 16
Second halfDue before October 16, with no second-half statement mailed
Mailed paymentOn time when the postmark shows the due date or earlier
Late penalty after the due date2% on homestead, 4% on nonhomestead
Delinquent statusTax still unpaid when the new year begins
Delinquent listPrinted in the newspaper each March

The Treasurer does not mail second-half statements, so keep the stub from the first one. Missing paperwork is no defense: the office says the owner is still responsible, and courtesy letters for unpaid current-year tax carry added penalty and fees. After the first jump, the statute adds one percent per month, up to 8% on homestead and 12% on nonhomestead land.

Under the same statute, a tax of $100 or less is due in one payment with the first half. Owners of small parcels should ask the Treasurer which threshold applies before paying.

Who pays what when an Aitkin County house sells?

On this point the Treasurer's FAQ is direct: delinquent taxes get paid at closing. The closing statement, or the realtor or attorney on the deal, will show how the current year is divided.

Escrow customers have a lender that receives the figures straight from the county. The copy mailed to the owner says in bold print not to pay, yet it remains useful at filing time and for refund claims. A buyer who closes after statements went out can get a copy online or from the Treasurer, and the county says that is the buyer's job.

Two state rules touch the deed itself. Statute 272.115 requires a certificate of value on sales above $3,000 and has the assessor remove homestead status after a sale unless the buyer applies and qualifies. Statute 287.21 sets the deed tax at 0.33% of net consideration above that figure.

A mobile home is handled separately. Its title cannot move until the taxes are paid, and relocating one takes a Mobile Home Clearance Sheet from the Treasurer.

Can Aitkin County homeowners get tax relief?

Two programs appear in the Treasurer's FAQ. The state property tax refund is claimed on form M1PR, available from the Department of Revenue.

The second is the Senior Citizen Property Tax Deferral. The county calls it a low-interest loan from the state and says it is not tax forgiveness. Homeowners aged 65 or older with household income of $60,000 or less can defer part of the tax, the state pays the county, and interest accrues. A seller already in the program should ask the Department of Revenue how a sale affects the deferred balance before listing.

If you cannot tell whether either program fits, the Treasurer at 218-927-7325 can say what to bring.

More questions about Aitkin County, MN Property Tax Guide

Which office answers questions on an Aitkin County tax bill?

The Treasurer, at 218-927-7325, handles billing, payments and statement copies, from an office at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119. For value or class questions, dial the Assessor at 218-927-7327.

Does Aitkin County accept mailed tax payments?

Yes. A payment counts as timely if the postmark meets the due date. Address it to the Treasurer at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119, Aitkin, MN 56431. The back of each stub has a form for changing the mailing address.

What if my Aitkin County tax statement never arrives?

You still owe the tax and the same penalties apply. A replacement copy can be printed online or requested from the Treasurer.

Must back taxes be cleared to close an Aitkin County sale?

Yes, delinquent taxes are paid at closing. Tax left unpaid into the next calendar year is delinquent, so ask the Treasurer for a payoff amount well ahead of the closing date.

Is there a way to contest value after the spring boards adjourn?

Yes, by petitioning the Minnesota Tax Court before April 30 of the taxes-payable year. The Assessor's appeals page says the court hears owners who never went to the local or county board.

Selling in Becker County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who to contact in Becker County

  • Becker County Auditor-Treasurer

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Assessor appointed by County Board and approved by MN Commissioner of Revenue; supervises assessments of all townships and cities (from the county site listing; confirm with the office)

Tax rate

Selling in Becker County?
We buy Becker County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Millage/tax rate not collected

Which Becker County offices run property tax?

Becker County divides the job between the Assessor and the Auditor-Treasurer. The Assessor is appointed by the County Board of Commissioners and approved by the Minnesota Commissioner of Revenue. That office supervises the assessments of every township and city in the county and keeps records on about 29,200 taxable properties and 3,339 tax-exempt ones.

Appraisal work is done by state accredited and certified staff from the county office, along with certified assessors hired by townships and cities. The county supplies value and classification schedules built from sales ratio studies, which the Assessor uses to equalize values between properties, taxing districts, school districts and neighboring counties.

The Auditor-Treasurer, an elected official, calculates rates, prepares statements and Truth in Taxation notices, collects the tax and county special assessments, and tracks unpaid parcels. Most Assessor records are public, apart from data covered by the privacy act.

What is the Becker County housing market like?

Becker County lies in northwest Minnesota, with Detroit Lakes as the county seat. It covers 1,445 square miles, of which 130 are water, making it the 15th largest Minnesota county by area. Several hundred lakes, farmland and forest share the landscape, among them Detroit Lake, Lake Sallie, Lake Maud, Lake Melissa and Big Cormorant Lake. The highest point is a hill near Wolf Lake at 1,861 feet.

The county was created on March 18, 1858 and organized in 1871. It carries the name of George Loomis Becker, one of three men elected to Congress at statehood. Minnesota could send only two, so Becker stayed behind and was promised a county. Colonel George Johnston founded Detroit Lakes in 1871 and the Northern Pacific Railroad fueled its early growth. An 1877 vote made Detroit the seat over Frazee, Lake Park and Audubon, and the Soo Line built through the county in 1903.

Census QuickFacts for the housing market:

  • 35,497 residents in July 2025, with 26.8 people per square mile of land
  • 20,440 housing units, and 77.2% of homes lived in by the owner
  • Median value of $291,000 for an owned home, with median rent at $920
  • Monthly owner costs of $1,691 with a mortgage and $580 without
  • 182 building permits in 2025, and retail sales of $21,864 per person in 2022

One in four residents is 65 or older, and 7.2% identify as American Indian or Alaska Native, and White Earth is among the county's census-designated places.

What does the Becker County assessment calendar look like?

The Assessor's timeline page lists duties through the year. The dates below are the ones a homeowner is most likely to need.

  • January 2 is the assessment date for real and personal property.
  • February 1 is the last day to file for exemption from taxation.
  • March 31: statements go out by this date from the Treasurer, except for manufactured homes.
  • April 1 to May 31: local boards of appeal and equalization hold their meetings, and value notices go out at least ten days ahead.
  • April 30: last day to file a Tax Court petition about current taxes.
  • June: the County Board of Appeal and Equalization meets during the last ten meeting days after the second Friday, with times printed on the valuation notice.
  • August 15: deadline for the Property Tax Refund, Form M-1PR.
  • Late November: Truth in Taxation notices go out, with public hearings in the weeks after.

December 1 is the last day for owners of real property to establish homestead for the year, though applications can be filed with the Assessor until December 15 to count for that year's assessment.

When are Becker County property taxes due?

Most owners pay in two installments, May 15 and October 15, but the county's own schedule lists several exceptions that depend on property class.

Becker County schedule of property taxes payable, by class and date (Auditor-Treasurer schedule)
DateWho it covers
May 15First half of real property tax; personal property tax
May 31First half for class 1c and 4c resorts and qualifying class 3a seasonal commercial property
August 31First half of manufactured home personal property tax
October 15Second half for non-farm real property
November 15Second half for farm real property and for manufactured homes

Statute 279.01 adds two details. When the statements miss an April 25 postmark, the first installment moves to 21 days after the postmark date. Class 3a seasonal property qualifies for the later date only if the owner attaches an affidavit showing more than 60 percent of gross income comes from May through August.

A homestead owner on federal active service as a National Guard or reserve member gets four extra months, moving a May 15 payment to September 15 and an October 15 payment to February 15, with a copy of orders or form DD214.

How do I pay Becker County property tax online?

The Auditor-Treasurer's page links to an online and phone payment service, and e-check or card payments through it carry extra fees. The county asks for specific identifiers so the payment is credited to the right parcel.

  • Bill number: five digits, leaving off the beginning zero, printed on the first-half and second-half stubs.
  • Parcel or property ID: all nine digits with no decimal points, so 01.0001.000 is entered as 010001000.
  • Jurisdiction code: 3308 identifies Becker County.

The same page offers a parcel and tax record search showing taxes, assessments, and land and building features, linked to the county's online mapping. Run it before you list to review the taxes and assessments on record for your parcel.

What is the Becker County appeal route?

Begin with the Assessor, because a conversation about the value notice often resolves a data error. If it does not, the local board is the next step. Statute 274.01 makes the town board or city council the local board unless the city has a charter board or has handed the job to the county. Someone who ignores a notice that the board plans to raise the assessment generally cannot go to the county board later.

The county board convenes in June. After that, a petition to district court or Tax Court under Statute 278.01 must be on file by April 30 of the taxes-payable year. Appeals of manufactured homes assessed as personal property run on a separate calendar, with a September 1 petition date.

What happens to Becker County taxes when I sell?

The Auditor-Treasurer touches the sale before the Recorder does. That office collects the state deed tax, mortgage registration tax and split fees on conveyances and enters each transfer in a permanent database before the document is filed with the County Recorder. Questions on the electronic certificate of real estate value go to the Assessor's chief deputy.

Unpaid tax carries consequences beyond penalties. The Auditor-Treasurer puts delinquent parcels into judgment, runs forfeiture proceedings and sales under statute, and may use revenue recapture to collect. A seller with a back balance should settle it before closing instead of leaving it for the buyer's title company to find.

A few programs affect timing. Senior citizens apply for the state's property tax deferral by July 1 for taxes payable the following year, and farmland owners file for Green Acres deferral by May 1. Resort owners declare class 1c or 4c status with the Assessor by January 15, and people who are blind or permanently and totally disabled apply to the Department of Revenue for the special homestead class by October 1.

More questions about Becker County, MN Property Tax Guide

Who is the Becker County Assessor appointed by?

The County Board of Commissioners appoints the Assessor, and the Minnesota Commissioner of Revenue approves the appointment. The office supervises assessments for all townships and cities in the county.

When is the second Becker County property tax payment due?

October 15 for non-farm real property. Second-half tax on farm real property, including split-class parcels that are partly agricultural, is due November 15, as is the second half for manufactured homes.

Do Becker County resorts pay property tax on a different date?

Yes, the schedule differs for them. Class 1c and 4c resort property and qualifying class 3a seasonal commercial property may pay the first half by May 31 instead of May 15, per the county schedule and Statute 279.01.

What do I need to pay Becker County taxes online?

You need the five-digit bill number from your payment stub, the nine-digit parcel number without decimal points, and the jurisdiction code 3308. E-check and card payments add fees.

Where do I send questions about a Becker County eCRV?

Contact the Chief-Deputy Assessor, who the county lists for tax estimates, agricultural questions and eCRV inquiries. The County Assessor handles exempt questions and sales inquiries.

Selling in Renville County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Renville County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who to contact in Renville County

  • Renville County Auditor-Treasurer

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Assessor office handles assessment records per MN statutes; every fifth year an appraiser inspects all properties (from the county site listing; confirm with the office)
  • Auditor-Treasurer is appointed official, liaison to 27 townships, 10 cities, nine school districts (from the county site listing; confirm with the office)

What we could not confirm

Where do you go for property tax questions in Renville County, MN?

Go to the Renville County Courthouse at 500 East DePue Avenue in Olivia. The Auditor-Treasurer, Heather Weis, is in Suite 202 (320-523-2071) and calculates and collects tax. The Assessor's office is in Suite 205 (320-523-3645), led by Doug Bruns, Director of Property Records and Taxpayer Services. Both open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

A drop box outside the courthouse's north door takes property tax payments around the clock. The Auditor-Treasurer also acts as liaison to 27 township boards, 10 city councils and nine school districts, which explains why one office can answer questions about who levies what on your parcel.

What kind of county is Renville County for a seller?

Renville County is a farm county of 987 square miles in the Minnesota River valley. The river runs along its southwestern border, Hawk Creek drains the west, and Beaver Creek drains the middle. Only Beltrami and Stearns Counties also touch nine neighbors. The territorial legislature created the county in 1855, and the seat moved from Beaver Falls to Olivia in 1900.

Olivia, with 2,343 people in 2020, calls itself the Corn Capital of the World and sits at the crossing of U.S. Highways 71 and 212. Its school system, BOLD, joins Bird Island, Olivia and Lake Lillian. The other cities are Bird Island, Buffalo Lake, Danube, Fairfax, Franklin, Hector, Morton, Renville and Sacred Heart. The county saw heavy fighting in the 1862 Dakota War at Birch Coulee in Birch Cooley Township.

Census QuickFacts give the housing picture:

  • 14,356 residents in July 2025, a 2.5% drop from April 2020, at roughly 15 people per square mile.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes of $163,200 for 2020 to 2024, with 80.2% of households owning.
  • Median gross rent of $790 and 6,056 households.
  • Ten building permits in 2025, and 23.9% of residents aged 65 or older.

Ask the Assessor how the value on your notice compares with recent sales near you, and bring photos of any condition problems the appraiser may not have seen.

When are Renville County property taxes due?

The county lists the first half of real estate tax as due May 15, the second half on residential property as due October 15, and the second half on agricultural property as due November 15. Both of the 2026 residential dates have passed. This year November 15 is a Sunday, so ask the Auditor-Treasurer before paying whether a payment received Monday, November 16 is on time.

Renville County real estate tax due dates, from the Auditor-Treasurer page
ClassFirst halfSecond half
ResidentialMay 15October 15
AgriculturalMay 15November 15

Minnesota Statutes section 279.01 treats a bill of $100 or less as due in full on the first date. A payment mailed and postmarked within one business day of a deadline earns a one-time penalty abatement, but only if you have not used that relief before.

How does the Renville County assessor value your home?

State law requires an appraiser to inspect every property in the county at least once every five years and to record features that affect market value, such as quality, condition, age and size. Each spring you receive a mailed notice listing the estimated market value from January 2 of this year, the value a year earlier and the classification. Next year's tax is figured from the value on that notice.

Homestead classification lowers the taxable value and requires paperwork:

  • You must own the home, live in it as your primary residence and be a Minnesota resident.
  • The application carries the Social Security number and signature of every owner who lives there, and of a resident spouse who is not on title.
  • Homeowners who hold an ITIN can now claim homestead, and the Assessor's office posts that notice in English and Spanish.
  • A farm owner of at least 40 acres who lives within four cities or townships of the land can qualify for an agricultural homestead by actively farming it.

How do you appeal a Renville County valuation?

Call the Assessor first, then go to the board that covers your township or city. In 2026 the township boards met April 6 through April 10 at halls from Sacred Heart to Winfield, and the City of Olivia board met Monday, April 20 at 6 p.m. in Olivia City Hall. All of those dates are over, and the county posted the 2026 schedule in February.

State law lets a town or city pass its board duties to the county, and the county must then offer an alternative review such as open book meetings in April and May (section 274.13). The 2026 Renville schedule included an open book session on Wednesday, April 8, from noon to 6 p.m. at the Assessor's office, covering fourteen townships and nine cities. If you miss the spring window, section 278.01 lets you petition the district court or Tax Court, with a filing deadline of April 30 of the tax year.

What happens to unpaid tax in Renville County?

Tax unpaid at the start of January is delinquent, and section 279.02 adds an extra 2% on the original amount at once. The Auditor-Treasurer's office also runs forfeited land proceedings, and its page carries a notice of expiration of redemption as of May 1, 2026.

The county's surplus notice shows what follows a sale. After the 2025 tax forfeited auction, one parcel had surplus proceeds of $5,516.50 with a claim deadline of June 9, 2026. Surplus is what remains once taxes, penalties, interest and costs are paid, and former owners have six months from the mailing of the notice to claim it. Forfeited parcels sold over the counter must be paid in full with a personal, cashier's or certified check or a money order made out to Renville County.

Does Renville County offer any tax relief for new building?

Yes. The Auditor-Treasurer administers a Tax Abatement Building Incentive Program meant to encourage new residential construction and the replacement of run-down houses. Call 320-523-2071 for the eligibility rules before you plan a teardown or a new build.

What should a Renville County seller check before closing?

Work through these before you sign a purchase agreement.

  • Ask the Auditor-Treasurer what is owed on the parcel and whether any special assessment, such as a ditch assessment, is attached.
  • Look up the parcel and your statement in the county's online property tax portal.
  • Confirm your homestead status and that the value on your spring notice is correct.
  • Expect the county auditor to certify that no delinquent tax exists before the deed is recorded, as section 272.12 requires.
  • File the certificate of real estate value for any sale above $3,000, as section 272.115 requires.

More questions about Renville County, MN Property Tax Guide

When is the second half due on Renville County farmland?

The county lists November 15. Because that day is a Sunday in 2026, confirm with the Auditor-Treasurer at 320-523-2071 whether Monday, November 16 counts as on time before you wait.

Can I pay my Renville County tax after hours?

Yes. A drop box outside the north door of the courthouse in Olivia is open 24 hours a day, and payments can go in it. You can also pay at the Auditor-Treasurer's office during business hours.

Which board hears appeals for a house in Olivia?

The City of Olivia local board of appeal and equalization, which met at Olivia City Hall at 6 p.m. on April 20 in 2026. Contact the Assessor at 320-523-3645 for the next date.

Can I claim homestead in Renville County with an ITIN?

Yes. The Assessor's office says homeowners with an ITIN can homestead their home. Stop in or call 320-523-3645 for the application, and expect to list every owner who lives in the home.

How long can a former owner claim surplus after a Renville County tax forfeiture sale?

Six months from the date the surplus notice is first mailed to that owner. The county mails the notice and a claim form by certified mail. Questions go to 320-523-2071.

Rice County by the numbers

Which Rice County offices deal with property tax?

Taxes are paid at the Rice County Property Tax & Elections Office on the second floor of the Government Services Building, 320 Third St. NW in Faribault (507-332-6104). Valuation questions go to the Assessor's Office at 507-332-6102. Joshua Schoen is the County Assessor.

The counter accepts cash, checks and money orders only, so cards must be used online or by phone. The Recorder handles the deed after a sale from the same building, and the county's Beacon site lets you search parcels and print your property tax statement.

What sets Rice County apart for a house seller?

Rice County is the most populous of the three Minnesota counties in this series, and it leans toward the Twin Cities. It covers 516 square miles, 20 of them water, in the south central part of the state. The Cannon River crosses the middle, the Straight River joins it in Faribault, and the North Fork of the Zumbro starts in the southeast. The county was founded on March 5, 1853 and named for fur trader Henry Mower Rice.

Faribault, the county seat, had 24,453 residents in 2020 and has Interstate 35 along its western edge. Northfield, home to Carleton College and St. Olaf College, had 20,790 and straddles the line with Dakota County. The other cities are Dennison (partly in Goodhue County), Dundas, Lonsdale, Morristown and Nerstrand, plus the Warsaw census-designated place. The county forms the Faribault-Northfield micropolitan area, part of the Twin Cities combined statistical area.

Census Bureau QuickFacts put numbers on the housing market:

  • 69,939 residents in July 2025, up 4.2% from April 2020, at 135.3 people per square mile.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes of $320,200 for 2020 to 2024, roughly double the value in Redwood or Renville County.
  • Median owner costs of $1,922 a month with a mortgage, and median gross rent of $1,083.
  • 76.3% owner-occupied, 25,596 housing units and 100 building permits in 2025.

What are the Rice County property tax due dates?

Non-agricultural real estate pays on May 15 and October 15. This year the October 15 deadline has passed, and the county's notice lists Monday, November 16 as the last 2026 deadline, for second-half agricultural property and mobile homes.

Rice County property tax installments, from the county's Pay Property Taxes page
Classification1st installment2nd installment
Real property, non-agriculturalMay 15Oct. 15
Real property, agriculturalMay 15Nov. 15
Personal propertyMay 15None
Mobile homeAug. 31Nov. 15

A yearly total of $100 or less, or $50 or less for a mobile home, must be paid in full on the first date. Under section 279.01, a missed deadline brings 2% on homestead and 4% on nonhomestead property. A second charge of the same size follows on the first of the next month, and then 1% a month through December up to caps of 8% and 12%.

How do you pay Rice County property tax, and what does it cost?

Paying by e-check or from a checking or savings account carries no fee. The ways to pay are:

  • Online through the Pay Property Taxes page: a 2.4% convenience fee with a $2 minimum applies to credit cards, and $4 to Visa debit.
  • By phone at 1-877-690-3729, using jurisdiction code 3321 and your property ID number. Wait for the confirmation number or the payment does not complete.
  • A quarterly or semiannual ACH plan, with enrollment forms on the county website.
  • By mail, with your check and payment stub, to the Property Tax & Elections Office at 320 Third St. NW, Faribault, MN 55021.
  • Through your lender's escrow account, if taxes are part of your mortgage payment.

How does Rice County decide what your home is worth?

The assessment date is January 2. The Assessor reviews annual sales studies to check how its estimated market values compare with real sales, and the Minnesota Department of Revenue requires those values to land between 90% and 105% of actual market value. New construction is valued in full or part depending on how far along it was on January 2.

The March 2026 mailing carried two papers. One was a Notice of Valuation and Classification for taxes payable in 2027, and the other was the 2026 tax statement, which lists each taxing body and county fees. The fee for solid waste service rose to $60 for any parcel with a building valued at $5,000 or more, the first increase since 2012. Owners of several buildings or units pay $60 for each, and commercial buildings use a formula the county board approved.

How do you appeal a Rice County property value?

Contact the Assessor at 507-332-6102 first. The 2026 open book meeting ran Monday, April 6 from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. at the Government Services Building, where owners could talk one on one with an assessor, and the county says many issues are settled there. Rice County's three local boards of appeal, for Forest, Shieldsville and Wells Townships, met at 9 a.m. on April 7, 8 and 9. Where a local board exists, your appeal must start there before it can move to the county board.

The County Board of Appeal and Equalization met on Wednesday, June 17, 2026 at 6:30 p.m. in the Commissioners Room. Section 274.13 bars that board from cutting the county's total assessed value by more than one percent. If you think the 2026 valuation is right, you do not need to attend anything.

How does Rice County tax affect a sale in Faribault, Northfield or the townships?

The buyer inherits the parcel, but the unpaid balance is yours. When the first business day of January passes with tax unpaid, section 279.02 adds 2% and the parcel is delinquent. Section 272.12 then stops the Recorder from accepting a deed until the auditor certifies that nothing delinquent is owed. For that reason a Rice County closing normally includes a payoff of whatever remains.

Northfield and Dennison cross county lines, so confirm which county your parcel sits in before choosing an office. The county named on your tax statement tells you which offices apply.

What should a Rice County seller prepare?

  • Print your 2026 statement from Beacon and check what has been paid.
  • Call 507-332-6104 if your mailing address has changed or a statement never arrived.
  • Compare your 2026 valuation notice with what similar homes sold for, because it sets 2027 tax.
  • Ask whether the $60 solid waste fee appears for each building on the parcel, and keep the figure in mind when you compare Rice County carrying costs with a buyer's budget.
  • Tell your closing agent which payment method you plan to use, since the counter cannot take cards.

More questions about Rice County, MN Property Tax Guide

What does it cost to pay Rice County property tax by credit card?

A 2.4% convenience fee, with a minimum of $2. Visa debit carries a flat $4 fee, and e-check payments have no fee. Cards work online or at 1-877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 3321.

Can I pay with a card at the Rice County counter?

No. The Property Tax & Elections counter accepts cash, checks and money orders only. For a card, pay online or use the phone line.

What is the $60 fee on my Rice County statement?

It is the solid waste service fee, charged on parcels with a building valued at $5,000 or more. It funds recycling, household hazardous waste, composting and waste reduction. Owners of several units pay $60 per unit.

Where do I appeal if my Rice County township has no local board?

Call the Assessor at 507-332-6102 and attend the open book meeting, then the County Board of Appeal and Equalization. Read your valuation notice, which lists every appeal option for your jurisdiction.

Is another Rice County property tax payment due before year end?

Yes, only for agricultural property and mobile homes: Monday, November 16, 2026. The second half on regular real estate was due October 15, and the next first half comes in May.

St. Louis County, MN Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • St. Louis County, MN Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • Louis County, MN Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the St. Louis County, MN Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in St. Louis County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy St. Louis County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who to contact in St. Louis County

  • St. Louis County Auditor

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Online payment via Paymentus (vendor domain ipn.paymentus.com): e-check free; credit cards 2.35%; Visa debit $3.95 per payment type

Tax rate

Selling in St. Louis County?
We buy St. Louis County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Millage/tax rate not researched

St Louis County by the numbers

Why is St. Louis County so big, and which office bills its tax?

No other county east of the Mississippi River is larger, and here the Auditor sends the bills while the Assessor sets the values. The county covers 6,860 square miles, 612 of them water, with Duluth as the seat. The name comes from the St. Louis River, which empties toward Lake Superior in the southeast corner. Census QuickFacts puts the density at 32 people per square mile of land.

According to the county's history page, most of Minnesota's iron mines are here, and they supply 85% of the country's domestic iron. The Port of Duluth-Superior handles more tonnage than any other Great Lakes port. Courthouses were built in Duluth in 1909 and in Virginia the next year. That two-city layout shows up in county services: the Auditor's office works from the Duluth Courthouse, the Mall-Service Center and the Government Services Center in Virginia, while property tax payments alone can also be made at the Hibbing Courthouse through the County Recorder.

Tax Division contact is 218-726-2383, at 100 N. 5th Ave. W. in Duluth. The Assessor's page lists what that office leaves alone: collecting taxes, calculating them, setting rates and writing property tax law. Its job is market value and classification.

What do the numbers say about housing in St. Louis County?

This is a county with an older population, steady headcount and modest home prices. QuickFacts puts July 2025 at 200,518 people, almost level with the 200,227 counted at the April 2020 base.

  • 105,503 housing units and 87,115 households, with 71.2% owner-occupied
  • Owned homes sit at $221,400 in the middle, and gross rent in the middle is $1,013
  • The middle household earns $70,069, and 12.7% of people live in poverty
  • 23.4% of residents are 65 or older, against 17.8% under 18
  • Builders took out 412 permits in 2025, and the average drive to work lasts 19.9 minutes

With 6,247 square miles of land and only 32 residents per square mile, a parcel's location inside the county shapes its value and its tax. That is one reason the assessment and appeal steps below matter to a seller.

Which days does St. Louis County collect property tax?

Real estate and personal property tax split into May 15 and October 15 payments. Farmland waits until November 15 for its second half, and resort property's first half runs to May 31. Weekend deadlines roll to Monday, and a mailed check needs a postmark no later than the deadline.

Statements go out in March, and state law sets March 31 as the cutoff. If none shows up, the owner has to ask the Tax Division for a duplicate. The office never forwards mail, so a returned statement just comes back to Duluth. Partial payments are welcome and are applied first to that year's accrued penalty.

  • E-check payments online through Paymentus are free, and the Auditor's page lists the other methods with their fees.
  • Drop boxes at county locations take checks or money orders, but no cash.
  • A Truth-in-Taxation notice arrives in November and shows the proposed tax for next year, with dates for local budget meetings.

The county also warns residents about a series of videos claiming a "Senior Homeowner Tax Review Request" tied to a federal law change. It says the programs and forms described do not exist, and it points owners to the real state programs through 218-726-2304.

What are the steps to appeal a St. Louis County valuation?

First speak with your assessor, then work through up to three levels in order, unless you go straight to Minnesota Tax Court. The county's appeals page spells out each level.

  1. City or township Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, which meets in April or May and can change your value or class. Contact the clerk to appear, or send a letter to the clerk to be read at the meeting. The meeting date is the deadline.
  2. County Board of Appeal and Equalization, in the last two weeks of June, made up of members with extensive real estate knowledge. Book a slot through the Clerk of the County Board at 218-726-2385.
  3. Minnesota Tax Court, with until April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

Unorganized townships skip the first level and appeal straight to the county board. The Tax Court has a Small Claims Division for homesteads of any value, other property under $300,000 in market value, and disputes of $5,000 or less including penalty and interest. The Regular Division hears everything else and follows civil procedure rules, so most owners there hire a lawyer. St. Louis County accepts service of Tax Court petitions in person or by email, and the petitioner must file with the district court on time.

What if St. Louis County property tax is not paid?

The county FAQ describes a slow but firm path. Tax left unpaid becomes delinquent on the first business day of January, and for a homestead the whole process generally takes up to three years.

Steps after St. Louis County property tax goes delinquent (Auditor FAQ)
StepWhat the county says
DelinquencyFirst business day of the year after the tax was due
NoticesTwo newspaper notices, the first by March 20, plus a mailing to the owner
Contest window20 days from the second notice to contest in District Court
Judgment and saleJudgment entered in May, tax judgment sale on the second Monday in May
Redemption3 years for homestead property under the 2014 rule
ForfeitureWhen redemption ends or 60 days after the last warning, whichever is later

Paying all delinquent tax and fees before redemption ends stops the process. The payment plan is called a confession of judgment. The owner pays one tenth of the delinquent tax, penalties and fees plus the current year's tax, and then pays the rest over up to 10 years for a homestead. After forfeiture the owner may be able to repurchase, but there is no guarantee, and the owner receives none of the proceeds if the county sells the land.

What tax steps come first when I list a St. Louis County house?

Call the Tax Division at 218-726-2383 and request the current balance, including penalty and any special assessment, well ahead of closing. Special assessments for improvements such as streets appear on the statement as a separate amount, and they are based on the benefit to the property, not its value.

Some parcels here have extra layers. The county's FAQ explains that Tax Increment Financing districts divert part of the tax to the district without changing how the bill is figured, and fiscal disparities share a portion of commercial and industrial growth with the seven-county metropolitan area. If a buyer or title company asks about either, the Auditor's Tax Division can say whether a parcel is affected.

The county's Mortgage/Deed Tax Calculator is linked from the Auditor's page, and the Recorder's office notes that property in the county is either Abstract or Torrens title, which affects how documents are recorded. The office does not give legal advice or help prepare documents, so direct questions to a real estate attorney or a practicing abstractor.

More questions about St. Louis County, MN Property Tax Guide

What are the St. Louis County tax deadlines?

May 15 for the first half and October 15 for the second half of real estate and personal property tax. Agricultural second halves are due November 15, and the postmark must show the due date or earlier.

How do I book a hearing before the St. Louis County board of appeal?

Call the Clerk of the County Board at 218-726-2385. The County Board of Appeal and Equalization meets in the last two weeks of June, after the city or township board has acted.

Is there a free way to pay St. Louis County tax?

Yes, e-check payments through Paymentus are free. Other online methods carry fees listed on the Auditor's page, and checks or money orders (no cash) can go in a county drop box.

What is the redemption period for a delinquent St. Louis County homestead?

Three years for homestead property under the rule effective in 2014. You may pay all delinquent tax and fees at any time before redemption ends, or enter a confession of judgment payment plan.

Where does an unorganized township owner appeal in St. Louis County?

Directly to the County Board of Appeal and Equalization, because those townships have no local board. Call the Clerk of the County Board at 218-726-2385 to book a time.

Selling in Steele County? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who to contact in Steele County

  • Steele County Finance / Treasurer

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Direct payment forms must be received by Treasurer by April 30 (1st half) and Sept 30 (2nd half) (from the county site listing; confirm with the office)

Selling in Steele County?
We buy Steele County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What we could not confirm

  • Millage/tax rate not researched

Which Steele County office do I call about my tax bill?

Call the Property Tax and Elections office at 507-444-7410 for the tax calculation and records, and the Finance office at 507-444-7420 for payments. Both work from the County Administration Building at 630 Florence Avenue in Owatonna, and mail goes to P.O. Box 890, Owatonna, MN 55060. The Assessor's Office, at 507-444-7435, handles value and classification.

The Property Tax and Elections page lists what that office does: it works out the tax capacity rates, computes the tax on each parcel from the budgets of the county, townships, cities and school districts, assigns special assessments, processes deed transfers and keeps delinquent tax records. It also runs Confession of Judgment contracts for owners behind on a bill, handles county ditch records and collects the aggregate tax.

The county mails real estate statements each March and mobile home statements each July. Every owner gets a statement, including owners whose lender pays through escrow, so a seller should be able to find the current one.

What should a Steele County seller know about the county itself?

Steele County is a small, mostly agricultural county in southern Minnesota with Owatonna as its seat and largest city. The county describes itself as 432 square miles, about 24 miles long and 18 wide, with four cities (Owatonna, Medford, Blooming Prairie and Ellendale) and thirteen townships. The Straight River flows north through the middle, and Rice Lake State Park, Beaver Lake and Oak Glen Lake are the named waters.

The territorial legislature carved the county out of Rice, Blue Earth and Le Sueur counties in February 1855 and named it for Franklin Steele. Owatonna, settled in 1854, became the seat. Interstate 35 passes Medford, Owatonna and Ellendale, U.S. 14 and U.S. 218 meet near Owatonna, and Minnesota 30 crosses the south. Owatonna Degner Regional Airport lies northwest of town.

The terrain is low rolling hills devoted to farming wherever the soil allows. For sellers, that means a mix of town lots, acreage inside township lines and farmsteads, and each of those has a different local board, a different set of special assessments and sometimes a different tax class.

What do Steele County's housing figures look like?

Roughly 79 percent of Steele County homes have an owner living in them, and the median household income is above $84,000. The table gives the Census Bureau's current QuickFacts figures.

Steele County at a glance, from QuickFacts
ItemFigure
Population, July 1, 202537,464
Change since 20200.1%
Housing units16,309
Owner-occupied rate79.4%
Median owner-occupied value$245,400
Median gross rent$1,061
Median household income$84,196
Building permits, 202554

Population has barely moved since 2020, and only 54 building permits were counted last year.

When are Steele County property taxes due in 2026?

The second half of 2026 real estate tax was due October 15, and second-half agricultural tax is due Monday, November 16, because November 15 fell on a Sunday. The county's payment page prints the 2026 dates and says a weekend due date rolls forward to the following business day.

Steele County 2026 payment dates from the county Finance page
DateWhat is due
January 1, 2026Unpaid 2025 tax becomes delinquent
May 15, 2026First half real estate
August 31, 2026First half mobile home
October 15, 2026Second half real estate
November 16, 2026Second half agricultural

An owner of farmland should confirm that date with the Finance office. The drop box in front of the Administration Building takes payments until 8:00 a.m. on the business day after the due date. After that hour the payment must include the penalty.

How can I pay a Steele County tax bill?

You can pay in person, by mail, at the drop box, by card or e-check, or through direct debit. The Finance office is on the first floor of the Administration Building and keeps weekday business hours.

  • In person at 630 Florence Avenue, Owatonna, on weekdays except federal holidays.
  • By mail to Steele County Finance, P.O. Box 890, Owatonna, MN 55060.
  • Online or by phone through the Tax Information and Parcel Data link. The fees are 2.5 percent of the tax, with a $1.50 minimum, for a credit or debit card, $3.95 flat for a Visa debit card, and $1.50 for an e-check under $10,000 or $10.00 above that.
  • Direct debit in two installments with no convenience fee. Forms are due in the Finance office by April 30 for the spring half and September 30 for the fall half.

Save the confirmation of any electronic payment, since the county asks owners to keep it.

Where does a Steele County owner take a value dispute?

Talk to the Assessor's appraiser first, then appear before the local board of appeal and equalization, then the county board if needed. In 2026 the township boards met between April 6 and April 16, and open book sessions ran on April 8 in Blooming Prairie, April 15 in Medford and April 22 at the Administration Building. The county board met on June 16 at 7:00 p.m., so this year's window has closed.

The county tells owners that a reduction has to be backed by facts, because a lower value moves tax onto other property. The assessor values each parcel as of January 2 at its usual selling price under Minnesota Statutes 272.03. The county's property tax programs page lists the special agricultural homestead, the market value exclusion for veterans with a disability, the special homestead for blind or disabled owners, Green Acres and Rural Preserve, exempt property and a senior deferral.

What does Steele County require to record a sale?

A deed recorded in Steele County must carry the deed tax, an electronic certificate of real estate value number and a well disclosure. The Recorder's checklist spells out each item for a transfer deed.

  • Deed tax is the purchase price times 0.0033, and the eCRV number goes on the first page when the price is $3,000 or more.
  • The well disclosure certificate costs $54, unless the seller uses one of the two statements the checklist allows.
  • The deed must name where to send tax statements, and grantors must state their marital status.
  • Properties with delinquent taxes may not be transferred.

If you plan to split a parcel before the sale, the county charges $100, requires all current-year taxes paid on every parcel involved, and asks for a survey on rural land under 40 acres. A parcel inside a city also needs that city's approval.

Which other Steele County offices matter before closing?

Four other county numbers are worth keeping beside the tax statement. The Recorder's Office at 507-444-7450 files the deed and answers questions about the checklist. Planning and Zoning and Environmental Services share 507-444-7475 and cover building permits and land-use rules in the townships. The GIS office at 507-444-7489 maintains the parcel maps, and the Assessor's Office posts an annual calendar and a frequently asked questions sheet for owners.

Ditch assessments are another item that can ride on a rural parcel. The Property Tax and Elections office keeps the county ditch records and files ditch liens and maintenance assessments, so a farm or acreage seller should ask whether the parcel sits in a county drainage system. The same office also collects the aggregate tax and holds the tax-forfeited land process, though the county's forfeited property page currently lists no parcels for sale.

For a first conversation, bring the parcel number from your statement. Every one of these offices keys its records to it.

More questions about Steele County, MN Property Tax Guide

What is the Steele County Assessor's phone number?

507-444-7435. The office is in the County Administration Building at 630 Florence Avenue, Owatonna, and handles value and classification questions.

Does Steele County mail a second-half tax statement?

Check the statement you received in March. The county mails real estate statements once a year in March and lists both halves on it, with special assessments shown on line 13.

Can I use the drop box for Steele County property tax?

Yes. It sits in front of the Administration Building next to the flagpoles, and payments are accepted through 8:00 a.m. the next business day after the due date. Later payments owe a penalty.

What is the deadline for paying delinquent Steele County tax before forfeiture?

Unpaid tax turns delinquent every January 1 after its due year, and the owner then has either one or three years depending on the property's classification. Ask the Property Tax office at 507-444-7410 which applies.

Are any Steele County tax-forfeited properties for sale?

The county's forfeited land page currently says no properties are for sale. Call 507-444-7410 or stop in at the Administration Center for terms of sale.

Who to contact in Itasca County

Tax rate

Selling in Itasca County?

What we could not confirm

  • Millage/tax rate not researched

Itasca County by the numbers

Where do I deal with property tax in Itasca County?

Both the Assessor and the Auditor/Treasurer work out of the Itasca County Courthouse at 123 NE 4th Street in Grand Rapids, ZIP 55744, with weekday hours that end at 4:30 in the afternoon. The Auditor/Treasurer is on the second floor.

The Assessor finds, lists and values every taxable parcel, calculates net tax capacity by property class, mails owners their value and classification, and holds the local and county boards of equalization. The Auditor/Treasurer sends statements and takes payment. The Assessor's phone is 218-327-2861 and the Treasurer's is 218-327-2860.

What sets Itasca County apart from a typical Minnesota county?

Itasca County is a big, wooded, lake country in the Iron Range region, with Grand Rapids as the county seat. It is Minnesota's third-largest county by area: 2,928 square miles in all, 2,668 of them land.

Wikipedia counts more than 1,400 lakes, including Lake Winnibigoshish, Pokegama Lake, Deer Lake and Bowstring Lake, plus the Mississippi River, which crosses the county. Forests of pine, spruce, hardwood, cedar and tamarack cover much of it, and forestry and logging remain major parts of the local economy. Part of the Chippewa National Forest lies inside the county, as do parts of the Bois Forte and Leech Lake reservations.

For July 2025 the Census Bureau estimates 45,404 residents, a gain of just 0.9% on the 2020 base, spread over a land area of 2,667.74 square miles. That works out to 16.9 people per square mile. Residents skew older here: 27.7% are 65 or over.

  • Housing units: 26,005 in July 2025, with 249 building permits in 2025.
  • Owner-occupied rate: 83.0%, 2020 to 2024.
  • Typical owner-occupied home: $225,200 at the median.
  • Median household income: $68,603, and median gross rent: $988.

The 2020 census recorded 25.2% of Itasca housing units as vacant, the highest share among the four counties in this series.

How is Itasca County organized, and does it change who values my house?

Itasca's boundaries were first set in 1849 when Minnesota Territory was created, and the county once covered land that is now Cook, Lake, Koochiching and parts of several others. It takes its name from Lake Itasca, the source of the Mississippi, though that lake is outside today's borders.

Today the county is divided into dozens of townships, among them Bigfork, Bowstring, Deer River, Grand Rapids, Marcell, Nashwauk, Trout Lake and Wawina, plus unorganized territories. Because the Assessor's page says the county office handles valuation for all taxable property in Itasca County, a seller in a far-flung township still starts at the courthouse in Grand Rapids for value and classification questions. Where a city assessor also works in your area, the statute says the county assessor forwards a petition copy to that authority, so ask which office issued your notice.

When are Itasca County property taxes due?

A residential bill splits into May 15 and October 15 payments. Resorts, manufactured homes and agricultural land keep their own dates, and a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday pushes any of them to the following business day.

Itasca County payment due dates
Due dateTax type
May 15Real property, first half (or whole bill if $100 or less)
May 31Real property, resorts, first half
August 31Manufactured homes, first half (or whole bill if $50 or less)
October 15Real property, second half
November 15Agricultural real property and manufactured homes, second half

Source: Itasca County Payment Due Dates. Personal property and severed mineral interest taxes come due with the real property tax.

How can I pay an Itasca County tax bill?

You can pay by mail, online, by phone or in person. The county site says cash, check and debit or credit card are taken at the office, and a mailed check needs a postmark no later than the due date.

  • Card payments carry a 2.25% service fee with a $1.00 minimum.
  • An e-check through MuniciPay is a flat $1.00 per transaction under $100,000.
  • Phone payments go through 218-535-7880 and need the Property ID Number from the top left of the statement.
  • Online and phone payments take one to two business days to post.

The county also offers free automatic payment enrollment, with the same $1.00 ACH fee. If your taxes are in a mortgage escrow, the statement carries a note not to pay, and any change in the escrow agent has to come from the escrow company to the Auditor/Treasurer.

What does Minnesota add for late payment?

A missed installment draws a penalty of 2% on a homestead and 4% on anything else, per Minnesota Statutes section 279.01. A second step of the same size follows on the first of the next month, and one percent more is added monthly through December.

Caps apply at 8% for homestead and 12% for nonhomestead property. Agricultural homestead and certain rural land get a break on the second half only: no penalty attaches if it is paid by November 15. The same statute lets the county treasurer waive a penalty once when a mailed payment carries a postmark within one business day of the due date. Cabins and seasonal recreational property that are not used commercially get the homestead penalty rates, which matters in a county with this many lake properties.

How do I challenge an Itasca County valuation?

Talk to the Assessor first, then the local board in your city or township, then the county board. The Assessor's page describes this review as the first stage of appeals, with the Assessor appearing in tax court when needed.

If you still disagree, Minnesota Statutes section 278.01 lets you petition the district court by serving the county auditor and filing with the court administrator no later than April 30 of the tax-payable year. A Tax Court appeal is also open between receipt of the valuation notice and May 1. If a change in value or class reaches an owner only after February 28, the clock is 60 days counted from the day the notice was mailed.

The Assessor's page notes that the local board information was last updated on April 17, 2020, so call 218-327-2861 for this year's meeting schedule instead of relying on old postings.

What should an Itasca County seller do about taxes before closing?

Get a current statement or payoff from the Auditor/Treasurer for your parcel, and confirm whether the first and second halves of the current year are both paid. The county has its own parcel information system and an online statement lookup.

A house that sits at a lake, on forest land or in a township far from Grand Rapids may carry special assessments, so the county office is the place to confirm every line before a closing date is set. When a house is inherited, empty or behind on taxes, bring the parcel number and the latest statement and ask what is owed through the date you expect to close.

More questions about Itasca County, MN Property Tax Guide

When is the Itasca County first half due?

May 15 for regular real property. Resorts have until May 31 for the first half, and weekend or holiday dates roll forward.

What is the card fee for paying Itasca County taxes?

2.25% of the payment, with a $1.00 minimum. An e-check through the county's online service is a flat $1.00 per transaction under $100,000.

Where is the Itasca County Assessor?

In the Itasca County Courthouse at 123 NE 4th Street, Grand Rapids, MN 55744. Weekday hours run to 4:30 p.m., and the phone is 218-327-2861.

When is the court deadline to contest an Itasca County tax?

April 30 of the tax-payable year for a district court petition under Minnesota Statutes section 278.01. A Tax Court appeal can begin earlier, between the valuation notice and May 1.

Do manufactured homes in Itasca County follow the same calendar?

No. Manufactured homes pay the first half August 31 (or the whole bill if it is $50 or less) and the remainder November 15.

Selling in Mower County? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who to contact in Mower County

  • Mower County Auditor-Treasurer

Tax rate

Selling in Mower County?
