Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Millage/tax rate not researched

Mower County by the numbers

Which Mower County offices handle a property tax bill?

Two county offices share the work in Austin, and both sit in the Government Center at 201 1st Street NE. The Auditor-Treasurer in Suite 7 collects the money and is reachable at 507-437-9535. The Assessor in Suite 10 sets value and class and answers at 507-437-9440, Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM.

The Auditor-Treasurer page says the office collects real estate, personal property and mobile home taxes, then pays out each school district, city, township and special taxing district its share. The same desk collects special assessments that cities and townships levy for water, sewer, sidewalk, curb and gutter, septic and ditch repair.

Mower County runs what its Assessor calls a "true county assessor" system. County appraisers, not city or township assessors, value all of the roughly 21,300 parcels each year. That means one phone number covers every address in the county, from Austin to the smallest township.

What should a seller know about the county before pricing a house?

Mower County sits on the Iowa line in southeast Minnesota. Austin is both the county seat and largest city, and the county was created in 1855 and organized in 1856. It holds 14 cities and 20 townships laid out as a grid, five townships wide and four deep. The Cedar River crosses the western townships, and the Upper Iowa River starts here. Mower is one of only four Minnesota counties with no natural lakes, so waterfront premiums rarely come into play.

Census QuickFacts figures for the county:

  • 40,971 residents as of July 2025, up 2.3% from the April 2020 base
  • 17,120 housing units, with 77.6% lived in by their owners
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $185,200 (2020 to 2024 estimates)
  • Median gross rent of $927 and 2.52 people per household
  • Median household income of $73,074, and 136 building permits recorded in 2025

At a median under $200,000, a fixed repair bill or a back-tax balance takes a larger share of the sale price than it would in a county with higher values. Austin Municipal Airport sits east of the city, and Lake Louise State Park lies near Le Roy in the southeast corner.

Why would a Mower County appraiser come to my door?

Several routine programs put appraisers on the road, according to the Assessor's page. Appraisers wear reflective vests and drive county-branded vehicles, and they leave a card if nobody is home.

  • A five-year review of every parcel, normally run between May and September
  • Building permit reviews, done twice a year in November and January
  • Tax abatement inspections on new homes, required by the county's abatement policy
  • Reports of damaged or destroyed buildings, which owners are asked to call in so a structure that is gone stops being valued
  • Value appeals during April to June, which usually call for a full inspection of the property

Because November is a permit month, a recent addition or finished basement may already be on the appraiser's list. The county also hosts a free online parcel viewer that opens a two-page property card, tax statements and value notices for any parcel, searchable by parcel number, name or address.

How do I appeal my Mower County value?

Start with a call to your appraiser before the board date, because the Assessor says a full inspect is normally required to appeal. The 2026 notice, mailed in spring, set the value for taxes payable in 2027, and the spring meetings have now passed. The order matters next year:

  • Local board first. A township board hears appeals in the township, and the county's published April schedule had meetings from April 13 to 16, 2026. The county states you must appeal to the local board before the county board.
  • Open book instead of a meeting. Cities and some townships use open book, run in person or by phone at the Assessor's Office from April 6 to May 31, 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM. Austin city open book goes through the main office line.
  • County Board of Appeal and Equalization. It meets after the second Friday in June, made up of the County Board and the Auditor, and can change value or classification for the current year.
  • Minnesota Tax Court or district court. Under Minnesota Statutes 278.01, the petition must be filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

Only the estimated market value for the current assessment year is appealable, not the tax bill itself. Local boards also work under section 274.01, which caps their combined reductions at 1% of the assessor's total.

When are Mower County property taxes due and what are the penalties?

Taxes come due in two halves, mid-May and mid-October, with a later November date for qualifying farm land. The table below puts the deadlines and the late charges together.

Mower County payment deadlines and penalty steps under Minnesota Statutes 279.01
ItemRule
First halfPaid before May 16
Second halfPaid before October 16
Qualifying agricultural landSecond half penalty-free if paid by November 15
Opening penalty2% on homestead, 4% on nonhomestead
Ceiling after monthly additions8% homestead, 12% nonhomestead
Bills of $100 or lessWhole amount due with the first half

A mailed check is on time when the envelope is postmarked by the due date. A first-time late mailer who postmarks within one business day of the deadline can ask the treasurer to abate the penalty.

What happens if the tax is unpaid when I sell?

Unpaid current-year tax becomes delinquent on January 2 of the following year, according to the Auditor-Treasurer. First-year delinquent owners are notified, and the list appears in the newspaper each March while interest keeps running. Call 507-437-9456 for a payoff figure, since the office says the posted delinquent list may lag behind the current month.

After three years of non-payment a parcel can forfeit to the State of Minnesota. The office sends a Notice of Expiration of Redemption with a last chance to pay, and forfeited parcels are later sold at a county auction. Selling before that point is usually simpler than any redemption.

At transfer, Minnesota Statutes 272.12 has the county auditor check for delinquent tax on the land. The recorder will refuse the deed unless the auditor has marked it with the words "no delinquent taxes and transfer entered." A seller in Mower County who owes back tax therefore has to clear it at or before closing.

More questions about Mower County, MN Property Tax Guide

Who do I call in Mower County to pay or ask about a tax bill?

Call the Auditor-Treasurer at 507-437-9535, or 507-437-9456 for delinquent balances. The office is in Suite 7 of the Government Center, 201 1st Street NE, Austin. Questions about value or class go to the Assessor at 507-437-9440.

Does Mower County mail a valuation notice every year?

Yes, the county values all parcels annually and mails a Notice of Valuation and Classification each spring. The notice lists your local board or open book dates. Read both sides before calling your appraiser.

Can I appeal my Mower County property tax directly to the county board?

Not in most cases. The county says you must go to the local board of appeal first, unless your city or township uses open book, in which case the County Board is the next step. The Tax Court is open at any time before April 30.

Will an appraiser inspect my Mower County home before I sell?

Possibly. Five-year reviews run from May to September, permit checks happen in November and January, and appeals usually require a full inspection. Call 507-437-9440 if a card was left on your door.

What does the county do with parcels that stay unpaid for years?

Delinquent parcels are listed each March, and after three years of non-payment they can forfeit to the State of Minnesota. The county then holds a public auction so the land returns to the tax rolls. Owners get a Notice of Expiration of Redemption before that happens.

Who to contact in Pine County

What we confirmed on official pages

What we could not confirm

Which Pine County offices deal with a property tax bill?

Pine County splits the job between two courthouse-area offices. The Assessor (320-591-1632) puts a value and a class on about 32,000 parcels. The Auditor-Treasurer (320-591-1670) works out the tax from the levies of cities, townships, schools and the hospital district, then bills it, collects it and chases what goes unpaid. That office is at 635 Northridge Drive NW in Pine City, and both offices answer phones Monday through Friday, 8:00 to 4:30.

Appraisers are assigned by geography. One handles Clover and Sandstone townships and the cities of Pine City, Sandstone and Sturgeon Lake. Another has Hinckley, Chengwatana and Pokegama townships and the city of Hinckley. A third covers Barry, Crosby, Kettle River, Norman, Ogema and Pine City townships plus Rock Creek. Ask which appraiser holds your parcel before you dial.

Sellers lean on both. The Assessor's technicians process homestead changes and electronic certificates of real estate value after a sale, and the Auditor-Treasurer quotes what is owed against the parcel.

What kind of county is Pine County for a house seller?

Pine County lies along Minnesota's eastern border, where the St. Croix River separates it from Wisconsin. Of its 1,435 square miles, 1,411 are land. The Kettle River and the Snake River both drain toward the St. Croix, and between them the ground rolls in low hills, half forest and half farm field. Devil's Lake touches the southeast edge of Pine City, the seat. Fourteen cities fall inside the line, among them Hinckley, Sandstone, Rock Creek, Askov and Willow River.

The first Pine County took shape in 1856 and was named for its pine woods. Buchanan County and parts of Aitkin and Carlton counties were split off the next year, and the remainder was reorganized in 1872 with Pine City as its capital. Today Banning State Park and St. Croix State Park sit within it, along with a portion of Wild River State Park.

Census Bureau QuickFacts supplies the numbers a seller can price against. The county had 30,472 people in mid-2025, a 5.5% rise over 2020, and 17,905 housing units, of which 81.6% are owner-occupied. Owner-occupied homes carried a median value of $239,300 across 2020 to 2024. Households earned a median $71,146, workers drove 32.1 minutes on average, and builders pulled 213 permits during 2025.

Nearly a third of housing units were counted vacant in 2020, a sign of how many cabins and seasonal homes dot the lake and forest land.

What dates matter on the Pine County tax calendar?

The Assessor keeps a calendar of state-set deadlines. These are the entries that bite hardest for homeowners and people about to sell.

Pine County's tax year, drawn from the Assessor's dates page
WhenEvent
Jan. 2Value is fixed as of this day for the coming tax year
By Mar. 31Treasurer mails statements
Apr. 1 through May 31Local boards may hold their appeal meetings
Apr. 30Tax Court petition deadline for value or class disputes
May 15First installment deadline
Late JuneCounty board of appeal, on a date printed in your valuation notice
July 1Values lock for the year
Aug. 15State M-1PR refund claims close
Oct. 15Second installment on non-farm property and special assessments
Nov. 15Second installment for farm land and manufactured homes
Dec. 31Homestead must be in place by this date

The Auditor-Treasurer reminds owners that a statement that never showed up changes nothing about the due date, and an envelope postmarked on the due date is treated as paid on time.

How do I challenge my Pine County value or classification?

Start with a phone call and your spring valuation notice. Pine County's calendar lays out the road after that:

  • Ring the Assessor at 320-591-1632 and ask the appraiser for your township or city to look at the value or class again.
  • Present your case to the local board. Township boards and city councils may sit anytime from April 1 to May 31.
  • Move up to the county board in the back half of June. Your notice carries the date.
  • Use Minnesota Tax Court if the boards leave the dispute open, filing by April 30 of the payable year.

July 1 is the point where the county treats the year's assessments as closed, and only a statutory exception can reopen them.

Documents beat arguments. Bring a recent appraisal, a signed purchase agreement, or dated photos of roof, foundation or septic problems that an appraiser driving past would miss.

How can I pay Pine County property tax, and what happens when I am late?

Mail a check or money order to Pine County Auditor-Treasurer, 635 Northridge Dr NW, Suite 230, Pine City, MN 55063. A drop box faces the courthouse entrance, and the office specifically says no cash goes in it. Other routes are the county's online payment page, an automated phone line at 1-800-272-9829 (enter 3316 when asked for the Pine County code), and the counter. Card and e-check payments pass a service fee to an outside vendor, so check the amount before you pay that way.

Penalties start the day after a deadline. Statute puts the first jump at 2% for homestead and 4% for nonhomestead, with more added monthly. Once December ends, the county adds interest at 10% a year.

The county lays out what follows if the bill sits:

  • January 1: the balance counts as delinquent.
  • February 15: the parcel lands on a list filed with the court administrator, and the owner gets a letter.
  • By March 20: newspaper publication begins, with a repeat at least two weeks later.
  • Second Monday in May: judgment is entered and the parcel is bid in toward forfeiture, which in most cases leaves three years to redeem.

A confession of judgment turns the delinquent total into a five-year or ten-year payment plan, provided the current year's tax stays up to date.

What should a Pine County seller know about taxes at closing?

The Treasurer's counter collects current-year tax, deed tax and mortgage registry tax. For delinquent balances call 320-591-1670, and ask for the payoff in writing: the county warns that web figures can be off for owners on a payment plan.

State statutes shape the recording step. Under 272.12 the auditor must certify that no delinquent tax is owed before a recorder takes the deed. Section 272.115 requires a certificate of value whenever the price tops $3,000, and it has the assessor remove homestead for the following year unless the buyer qualifies. Section 287.21 sets the deed tax at .0033 of the net price above that threshold.

Manufactured homes run separately. A mobile home parcel will not move into the buyer's name until the title is transferred, and the county will not allow a title transfer while current or delinquent personal property tax remains.

Which Pine County tax breaks and refunds exist?

The county's FAQ sends homeowners to the Minnesota refund on Form M-1PR. The basic refund requires that you owned the home and lived in it on January 2. A separate special refund can follow when the tax on your homestead jumped more than 12 percent in one year. Forms are available from the Department of Revenue, and the Assessor's calendar fixes August 15 as the last filing day.

A few other deadlines on that calendar: October 1 for blind or permanently and totally disabled owners seeking special homestead status, May 1 for Green Acres and managed forest applications, and December 31 for the disabled veteran market value exclusion. Owners who are falling behind should phone the Auditor-Treasurer before forfeiture steps start. One small rule from the county board: overpayments under $5 are not refunded.

More questions about Pine County, MN Property Tax Guide

Which Pine County office gives a payoff for back taxes?

The Auditor-Treasurer, at 320-591-1670. Staff there calculate delinquent amounts and write confession of judgment contracts. Get the figure in writing, because web balances can be wrong for parcels on a plan.

Which installments does a Pine County homeowner owe each year?

Two: May 15 and October 15 for ordinary real property. Farm parcels and manufactured homes pay their second half on November 15, and manufactured homes pay the first on August 31.

Is it too late to contest a Pine County value in August?

Almost certainly. The county treats assessments as final once July 1 arrives, apart from changes a statute permits. Next year, work through the local board in April or May and the county board in June.

What happens if my Pine County statement is lost in the mail?

You still owe the tax on time. The county says a missing statement is no defense. Pull the parcel up on the county's online property site or ask the Auditor-Treasurer for a duplicate.

How do I claim the Minnesota refund on a Pine County homestead?

File Form M-1PR with the Department of Revenue by August 15. You must have owned and occupied the home on January 2. A larger special refund exists for tax increases above 12 percent.

Where do I go in Gaylord for Sibley County property tax questions?

Everything runs through the courthouse at 400 Court Avenue. The Auditor-Treasurer, on the first floor, mails and collects the bills (507-237-4070, P.O. Box 51, Gaylord, MN 55334). The Assessor, on the second floor, decides each parcel's market value and class (507-237-4078, P.O. Box 532), with counter hours of 8:00 to 4:30 on weekdays.

The Assessor's own page draws the line clearly: disputes over tax amounts or special assessments go to the Auditor-Treasurer, while value and classification stay with the Assessor. If you cannot print your current value notice or tax statement from the county's online portal, either office will send a copy.

What is Sibley County like for someone selling a house?

Think small towns and farm country along the Minnesota River. The county spans 601 square miles, 589 of them land, and its rolling hills are cut by creeks and dotted with ponds and small lakes. The Minnesota River marks the eastern edge, while the Rush River drains most of the lower county. Gaylord is both the seat and the largest city.

Henderson held the seat first, and its 1879 courthouse served until 1915, when Gaylord residents petitioned the supervisors for the change. That old building now houses Henderson's city offices. The other cities are Arlington, Gibbon, Green Isle, New Auburn and Winthrop, along with Le Sueur, which lies mostly in Le Sueur County. Census QuickFacts adds these figures:

  • A July 2025 estimate of 15,356 people, 3.4% more than the 2020 base.
  • 6,596 housing units, with 80.8% occupied by owners.
  • Owned homes valued at $231,900 in the middle of the range, while gross rent in the middle sits at $855.
  • The middle household earns $77,634, and 21.7% of residents past age 65.
  • The county has 5,929 households of about 2.5 people each, and 93.0% of residents lived at the same address a year earlier.
  • Just 28 building permits during 2025, and workers travel 27.1 minutes on average.

With so few new homes going up, most sales here involve houses that already exist.

Which Sibley County tax dates should I mark?

Spring and fall carry the main deadlines. Residential and commercial parcels pay in May and October, farmland pays its second half a month later, and the postmark on a mailed payment has to show the due date or earlier. When the date lands on a weekend, the following business day applies.

Payment calendar for Sibley County parcels (county Current Year Taxes page)
Type of taxFirst paymentSecond payment
Residential or commercial real estateMay 15October 15
Agricultural real estateMay 15November 15
Personal propertyMay 15, full amountNone
Mobile homeAugust 31November 15

Small real estate bills of $100 or under come due all at once with the first payment, leaving the second stub empty, and mobile home bills under $50 are due whole on August 31. State law sets a March 31 mailing deadline for statements, and the county sent its 2026 set out on March 20. Since October 15 has passed, search the online portal for any open balance on a parcel you are about to list.

What ways are there to pay a Sibley County bill?

Online or by mail is the county's preference, and it asks you to include every stub because the office takes no responsibility for parcels left unpaid. Payments are posted by parcel ID number.

  • Card or e-check: cards cost 2.35% of the amount (minimum $1.50) and e-checks cost a flat $1.50. By phone, call 507-237-4070 during the day or 855-414-3916 after hours.
  • Mail: use the envelope that came with your statement. The Postal Service now dates a letter when it receives it, so the county suggests mailing several days early or requesting a manual postmark at the counter.
  • Drop box: a locked box at the courthouse west entrance is emptied at 8:00 each morning, and earlier deposits count for the previous day.
  • Direct Payment Plan: free withdrawals on May 15 and October 15 or November 15. The county would like enrollment about three weeks before a payment date.

You can send a partial amount whenever you like. The whole half remains due on its date, but penalty builds only on the part still unpaid. Returned payments cost $30. Email reminders go out 10 to 14 days before each deadline if you ask, though the county says penalties apply even when a reminder never arrives.

How do I challenge a Sibley County valuation?

Expect a sequence of local board, county board and Tax Court. Values are fixed as of January 2, and the Assessor studies sales between October 1 and September 30 of the previous year to set them. The county says state guidelines expect assessed levels to sit between 90% and 105% of sale price.

  • Local board: townships and cities hold hearings from April 1 to May 31, and the Assessor attends to present data without a vote.
  • Open Book: where a jurisdiction passes its appeal power to the county, you meet the Assessor informally. Failing agreement there, you can go to the county board in June.
  • Tax Court: the assessment calendar sets April 30 as the final day to petition on a dispute that affects the current year's tax.

The county's board page says the owner carries the burden, because the assessor is presumed to have valued and classified correctly. Bring comparable sales, an appraisal or repair bids. A local board can raise or lower a value or change a class, but it cannot trim a whole township or city by more than 1%, and a mailed decision typically arrives within 10 days. Each parcel gets a physical look at least once every five years, announced by a spring postcard.

What happens to homestead status when a Sibley County house sells?

The seller must tell the Assessor within 30 days of the sale. The same rule covers moving out, a spouse moving out, or a change in marital status, and the county says a missed report can lead to the correct tax plus an equal penalty.

The buyer, if living there, files a new application by December 31 of the assessment year, and the county advises doing it soon after closing. A banner on the county home page repeats December 31, 2026 for this year. Forms go to the Assessor at the Court Avenue courthouse or to P.O. Box 532, and each owner must supply a Social Security or ITIN number.

Absence does not end homestead by itself. According to the county, an owner who goes south for the winter keeps it while the house stays maintained as a home awaiting return, and an owner who moves to a nursing home or assisted living keeps it as long as the house is maintained as the owner's homestead. Renting the house during an absence ends it, and so does claiming a second homestead elsewhere in Minnesota.

One more point from the county: a house that is rented, listed for sale or lived in by someone other than the owner becomes non-homestead for the following assessment year.

More questions about Sibley County, MN Property Tax Guide

Which dates matter for Sibley County real estate tax?

May 15 for the first half, then October 15 for residential and commercial second halves or November 15 for agricultural ones. Personal property is paid whole on May 15, and mobile homes follow August 31 and November 15.

Where can I find the Sibley County Assessor?

On the second floor of the courthouse, 400 Court Avenue, Gaylord, MN 55334. Phone 507-237-4078. The office is open weekdays from 8:00 am to 4:30 pm.

What fee applies to a card payment of Sibley County tax?

2.35% of the amount, with a $1.50 minimum, on credit or debit cards. An e-check carries a flat $1.50. Mail, the drop box and the Direct Payment Plan avoid those charges.

When will my Sibley County local board of appeal meet?

Sometime from April 1 through May 31, and your valuation notice lists the date. A county board hearing follows in June for anyone still unsatisfied.

Must I report the sale of my Sibley County home to the county?

Yes. Notify the County Assessor within 30 days of the sale. The office at 507-237-4078 can supply the form and answer questions.

The Assessor's Office carries about 24,500 real estate parcels. Staff view each property in person at least once every five years, and more often when there is construction or a recent sale.

What is Todd County like for someone selling a house?

Todd County is a central Minnesota farm and lake county of 980 square miles, with Long Prairie as its seat and largest city. About 945 square miles are land and 35 are water,. Wikipedia lists dozens, among them Big Swan, Sauk, Osakis, Birch and West Union lakes, and the terrain is rolling hills cut by drainages.

The Crow Wing River marks the northeast border, the Long Prairie River runs through the middle and the Wing River joins the Crow Wing. The Minnesota territorial legislature created the county in 1855, though county government was not organized until January 1, 1867. The name honors John Blair Smith Todd. Neighboring counties are Wadena, Cass, Morrison, Stearns, Douglas and Otter Tail.

The cities are Bertha, Browerville, Burtrum, Clarissa, Eagle Bend, Grey Eagle, Hewitt, Long Prairie, Osakis, Staples and West Union. Osakis is partly in Douglas County and Staples partly in Wadena County. Todd also has five Amish settlements, with seven church districts counted in 2013 and a total of about 1,000 people.

How does the Todd County housing stock look in the Census?

Todd County had 26,060 residents in 2025, up 3.1 percent from April 2020, and a very high share of homes are owner-occupied. The table gives the Census QuickFacts values.

Todd County homes and incomes, Census QuickFacts
ItemFigure
Population, July 1, 202526,060
Housing units13,427
Owner-occupied rate83.0%
Median owner-occupied value$207,700
Median gross rent$908
Median household income$67,662
Mean commute to work25.7 minutes
Building permits, 202584

The 2020 census counted 12,770 housing units, of which 22.5 percent were vacant. A seller of a lake cabin or other seasonal property should ask the assessor how the parcel is classified.

When are Todd County property taxes due?

On Todd County real estate, the first half is due May 15, the second half of commercial and residential property is due October 15 and the second half of agricultural land is due November 15. Todd's own payment page also lists personal property in full on May 15, and mobile homes on August 31 and November 15.

This year November 15 falls on a Sunday. The county says a due date on a weekend or legal holiday slides to the next working day, which puts the farmland second half on Monday, November 16. A mailed payment counts as on time if the postmark is on or before the due date. Under Minnesota Statutes 279.01, late homestead tax draws 2 percent and late nonhomestead tax draws 4 percent, with more added monthly.

The owner of a class 2a farm needs to watch one more rule. The statute lets agricultural homestead and nonhomestead land pay the second half by November 15 without a penalty.

How can I pay Todd County property tax?

You can pay online, by phone, in person, by mail or in the payment drop box. The box is at the street-level tunnel entrance of the Historic Courthouse at 215 1st Avenue South.

  • Phone: call 1-844-368-2607 for the automated Point N Pay system.
  • Online: Visa, MasterCard, American Express and Discover are accepted through the same vendor.
  • Convenience fees go to the vendor: 2.5 percent of the payment with a $1.50 minimum for most cards, $3.95 flat for Visa debit, and $1.50 for an e-check up to $10,000 or $10.00 above that.
  • Mail: send a check to the Auditor/Treasurer's Office. The postmark is the proof of timely mailing.

For parcel details on the current tax year and the current assessment year, the county provides a property information search portal. Use the same office numbers above if the portal figures look wrong.

How does the Todd County Assessor set a value?

The Assessor compares what properties actually sold for with their assessed values, then checks whether each district meets state requirements. Values are set as of January 2, and a notice goes to each owner in spring with the value, the classification and the steps to appeal.

Most records in the office are public, with exceptions for data covered by the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act. The Assessor also posts applications and forms online, and the county asks owners to call 320-732-4431 if a form they need is missing. A seller who disagrees with a notice should call that number before the spring meetings are set.

What is the appeal path for a Todd County property value?

Call the Assessor, appear before the local board, and then go to the county board. The county mails valuation notices each spring, with values set as of January 2, and the notice explains the appeal process. Ask the county for the date of this year's board of appeal and equalization meeting.

Under Minnesota Statutes 274.13 the county board can lower a value that is above market value, raise one that is below and change a classification, but it cannot grant an exemption. A person who gets a notice of a proposed increase and does not appear gives up the right to go to the state revenue commissioner on that value. Keep any evidence you collect, such as an appraisal or comparable sales, because the same case may apply next spring.

What does a Todd County seller do about the tax bill at closing?

Ask the Auditor-Treasurer for a statement of the current balance, then plan how the closing agent will split the year. Contracts usually have the seller cover the days they owned the home. The first half is due May 15 and the second October 15, so ask which of the two is still open on your closing date.

Look at special assessments too. The Auditor-Treasurer keeps those that the cities, townships and drainage systems certify, so a ditch lien or a street assessment may remain on the parcel after the sale. If the taxes are escrowed, ask the lender for its payoff letter, and give the Auditor-Treasurer the buyer's mailing address so the next statement arrives at the right place.

More questions about Todd County, MN Property Tax Guide

What is the Todd County Assessor's phone number?

320-732-4431. The Auditor-Treasurer, who handles statements and payments, is at 320-732-4469.

When is the Todd County farmland second-half tax due this year?

Monday, November 16, 2026. The usual date is November 15, but that is a Sunday and the county slides weekend due dates forward.

Can I mail a Todd County tax payment on the due date?

Yes. A postmark on or before the due date is the county's proof of timely mailing. A weekend or holiday due date slides to the next working day.

What does Todd County charge to pay by credit card?

The vendor charges 2.5 percent of the amount, with a $1.50 minimum, for most cards. A Visa debit card is a flat $3.95. The fees do not go to the county.

How many parcels does the Todd County Auditor-Treasurer bill?

About 23,000 parcels, according to the Auditor and Treasurer page. The Assessor's Office keeps records on roughly 24,500 real estate parcels.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who to contact in Dodge County

  • Dodge County Finance

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Assessor Ryan DeCook, (507) 635-6245, 721 Main St N, Mantorville MN 55955; hours 8:00-4:30
  • Appeals heard at Local Board of Appeal and Equalization or open book meetings in second half of April; only local board appeals can continue to County Board in June
  • Finance collects taxes; mail to Dodge County Finance, 721 Main St N, Dept. 45, Mantorville MN 55955; drop box available (from the county site listing; confirm with the office)
  • News page lists due dates (1st half real estate May 15, ag land Aug 31 listing unclear) (from the county site listing; confirm with the office)
  • Local board second half of April; county board June

Tax rate

Selling in Dodge County?
We buy Dodge County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Millage/tax rate not researched

Which Dodge County offices deal with property tax?

Two desks at the Government Services Building in Mantorville handle most questions: Land Records (the assessor) for value and classification, and Finance for the tax bill and payments. Both sit at 721 Main Street North, Mantorville, MN 55955, and the county posts weekday hours from eight in the morning until four-thirty.

  • Assessor (Land Records): 507-635-6245, Dept. 102. Ask here about estimated market value, classification, homestead and the appeal steps.
  • Finance: 507-635-6240, Dept. 45. Ask here about amounts due, duplicate statements, penalties and past-due balances.

Dodge County runs its parcel and payment lookup through an online tax portal, so you can search by parcel number or street address before you call. Lost statements can be printed from the portal for years back to 2013, and Finance mails duplicates by phone request.

Where does Dodge County sit, and who lives there?

Dodge County sits in southeastern Minnesota and belongs to the Rochester metropolitan area. Kasson is the largest city, while Mantorville holds the courthouse. The other cities are Blooming Prairie (shared with Steele County), Claremont, Dodge Center, Hayfield and West Concord.

The county was organized in 1855 and named for Henry Dodge. Its courthouse, built in 1865, is described as the oldest courthouse still in use in Minnesota, and Quarries around Mantorville once supplied cut stone, and Wasioja is known for its own stone. The land is about 24 miles long and 18 miles wide, rolling and fertile, with the South Branch of the Middle Fork of the Zumbro River crossing the upper middle.

The Census Bureau counted 20,867 residents in 2020 and estimated 21,376 for July 2025. QuickFacts lists 8,773 housing units, an owner-occupied rate of 86.6 percent, a median owner-occupied value of $287,700 and household income near $95,739 at the median for 2020 to 2024. Workers spend an average of 25.9 minutes getting to their jobs. With owners in nearly nine of ten occupied homes, a listing that arrives with an unpaid tax balance or an open classification question is easy for a buyer to spot.

When are Dodge County property taxes due?

Residential real estate tax is split into two halves, due May 15 and October 15, and farm land gets until November 15 for the second half. Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. 279.01) sets those dates and the penalties, so the county cannot waive them on its own.

The county reminds owners that a mailed payment needs a postmark dated no later than the due date. Its suggestion is to walk the envelope into the post office and ask for a hand stamp. A homestead payment that misses its date picks up 2 percent, and non-homestead picks up 4 percent. After the first of the next month the penalty climbs again, and from then on it adds 1 percent each month through December, up to a cap of 8 percent for homestead and 12 percent for non-homestead property. The state also lets the treasurer abate a first late penalty when a payment was mailed and postmarked within one business day of the deadline.

Dodge County property tax calendar. Sources: Dodge County Land Records important dates page; Minn. Stat. 279.01.
DateWhat happens
January 2Assessment date; unpaid prior-year tax becomes delinquent
March 31Last day Finance mails real estate tax statements
April 30Last day to file a Minnesota Tax Court petition for the current tax
May 15First half due
October 15Second half due, including special assessments
November 15Second half due on farm real property
December 1 and 15Own and occupy by December 1, apply for homestead by December 15

How do I pay a Dodge County tax bill?

You can pay by mail, at the Administration window, in a drop box, or online. Checks and money orders go to Dodge County, and the stub from your statement should travel with the payment. Mail goes to Dodge County Finance, 721 Main Street North, Dept. 45, Mantorville, MN 55955.

  • In person: Administration window on the main floor, paid by cash, money order, cashier's check or personal check.
  • Drop box: left of the west-facing main entrance. Write a note on the envelope if you want a receipt.
  • Online: card payments carry a 2.75 percent fee, and an e-check costs $3.99 per transaction. Plan on one to two business days for posting.

Finance sends no reminders. Only one statement per parcel goes out each year, and if you have not seen yours by April 10 the county asks you to call for a duplicate. Not receiving a statement does not remove the penalty.

How do I contest a Dodge County valuation?

Start with an appraiser at the assessor's office as soon as your spring Notice of Valuation and Classification arrives, because the assessor can change a value only until the local board convenes. After that, relief comes only from a board or the Tax Court.

  1. Local Board of Appeal and Equalization or open book meeting. Your city or township holds one in April or May, and the notice prints the date. Its reductions cannot lower the assessor's total for the district by more than one percent (Minn. Stat. 274.01).
  2. County Board of Appeal and Equalization. It meets in June. Only owners who appealed at the first level can be heard.
  3. Minnesota Tax Court. The petition is due April 30 of the year the tax is payable (Minn. Stat. 278.01). The Small Claims Division is final, while the Regular Division can be appealed further.

The county says plainly that a bill being too high is not a reason to adjust value. Bring a recent appraisal, comparable sales or errors in the property record instead. Tax-level questions belong at the December Truth in Taxation meetings.

How does homestead status work in Dodge County?

Homestead classification gives owner-occupied property a lower tax rate than similar non-homestead property. To get it, you present proof of ownership, complete an application and supply the Social Security numbers of all owners. You must also be a Minnesota resident and be listed as an owner on county tax records.

Timing matters for a buyer. A person who buys and moves in by December 1 and files by December 15 sees homestead rates in the following year's tax. A seller who rented the house out before listing may have changed the class, which is why Finance answers "why did my classification change" calls by sending people back to Land Records at 507-635-6245. Relatives of an owner can qualify too, as can certain trusts and life estates when the deed shows the interest.

How does tax get cleared when a Dodge County house sells?

The first thing the auditor checks at transfer is whether delinquent tax is owed. Under Minn. Stat. 272.12, a deed is presented to the county auditor, who looks for delinquent taxes and certifies the land clear before the recorder may accept the deed.

That is why a title company will ask for the payoff figure before closing. If you buy after statements have been mailed, Dodge County sends the new owner a courtesy letter showing the tax for the year rather than a full statement, and it does this even when a lender escrows the payment. A seller on a contract for deed stays responsible for confirming that taxes were paid, although only the new contract holder receives the bill. Ask the title or closing agent how the current year is divided between buyer and seller, since that depends on the purchase agreement.

What if back taxes are owed on a Dodge County property?

Call Finance at 507-635-6240 for the exact amount, which includes penalty and interest, or look the parcel up in the portal, where delinquent figures are kept current. Unpaid prior-year tax becomes delinquent on January 2.

Paying before listing usually simplifies the closing. If the amount is more than you can cover, ask Finance for the exact figure before the next January 2 so you know what the delinquency date will add.

More questions about Dodge County, MN Property Tax Guide

Where do I send a Dodge County property tax payment?

Mail it to Dodge County Finance, 721 Main Street North, Dept. 45, Mantorville, MN 55955, with the payment stub from your statement. The postmark must carry May 15 or October 15 or an earlier date, so the county suggests having the post office hand stamp it.

Is there a fee to pay Dodge County taxes online?

Yes. Card payments carry a 2.75 percent fee and an e-check costs $3.99 per transaction, with several parcels allowed in one e-check transaction. Allow one to two business days for the payment to post.

By when must a Dodge County owner file an appeal?

The local board or open book meeting comes first, in April or May, and the date is printed on your valuation notice. A Minnesota Tax Court petition has to be filed by April 30 in the tax-payable year.

I bought a Dodge County house after statements were mailed. Do I still owe the tax?

Yes. You will receive a courtesy letter from the county instead of a statement, and the tax is still yours to pay by the due dates. Call Finance at 507-635-6240 with your parcel number or address for a copy.

Which office changes my homestead status in Dodge County?

The assessor's office in Land Records, at 507-635-6245. File in person, by phone or by email, or download the form from the county website, and apply by December 15 after owning and living in the home by December 1.

Selling in Hubbard County? Get a Cash Offer

Who to contact in Hubbard County

  • Hubbard County Auditor/Treasurer

Tax rate

Selling in Hubbard County?

What we could not confirm

  • Millage/tax rate not researched

What should a seller know about Hubbard County?

Hubbard County is in northwestern Minnesota, with Park Rapids as the seat. It was created on February 26, 1883 from part of Cass County and named for Lucius Hubbard, governor from 1882 to 1887. The land is hilly, wooded and dotted with lakes, and parts of Itasca State Park, the Mississippi Headwaters and the Leech Lake Indian Reservation fall inside the county line. The cities are Akeley, Laporte, Nevis and Park Rapids.

The numbers from Census QuickFacts explain why property tax here looks different from the metro:

  • 22,369 residents in the July 2025 estimate, up 4.8% from the 2020 base.
  • 14,900 housing units but only 8,964 households, so a large share of homes are not a full-time residence. The 2020 census counted 39.6% of housing units as vacant.
  • 83.1% owner occupancy, a median home value of $282,600 and a median household income of $71,995.
  • 28.5% of residents are 65 or older.

A cabin or lake home that is used for part of the year is taxed differently from a primary residence, which is why classification is the first thing to check before listing.

Which Hubbard County office handles property tax?

Two departments share the work. The Auditor/Treasurer is responsible for property tax administration, delinquent taxes and the published delinquent tax list, and for forfeitures, repurchases and confessions of judgment. By statute the auditor also sits on the county board of equalization.

The assessor operates inside Property Records at the Government Center, 301 Court Ave., Park Rapids, MN 56470, phone 218-732-3552. Property Records covers valuation and classification, homestead, tax reduction programs and recording of real estate documents, so a single visit can cover a value question and a deed.

When are Hubbard County property taxes due and what are the penalties?

Minnesota Statutes 279.01 sets two halves, payable before May 16 and before October 16 when a parcel's tax is over $100. A parcel at or under $100 is due in full with the first half. A payment mailed and postmarked by the due date is on time, and the treasurer must abate the penalty once if the postmark falls within one business day after.

Late payment penalties under Minnesota Statutes 279.01
StageHomesteadNonhomestead
Day after the due date2%4%
First day of the next monthAnother 2%Another 4%
Each month after, through December1% more1% more
Ceiling8%12%

Agricultural homestead and qualifying farm land can pay the second half through November 15 without penalty. Seasonal residential recreational property that is not used commercially, the statute's class 4c, takes the homestead penalty rates.

How does homestead work for a Hubbard County buyer or seller?

The county has posted a homestead notice for the 2026 assessment. An owner who bought or moved into a home in the past year must apply by December 31, 2026 to have the benefit apply to taxes payable in 2027, and the applicant must have owned and lived in the home by that date. A qualifying relative living there also counts. For residential and agricultural property that list takes in the owner's or spouse's child, grandchild, sibling or parent, plus the owner's uncle, aunt, nephew or niece.

  • Applications can be filed online, in person or by mail, and once granted they are not repeated unless the assessor asks.
  • Every occupant, owner and spouse signs and gives a Social Security number so the state can check that no other Minnesota homestead is claimed.
  • The driver's license must show the home address, since Minnesota requires an address change within 30 days.
  • A relative homestead does not qualify for the property tax refund, and a property that was ever classified seasonal residential recreational under the current owner cannot take a relative homestead.

A seller who moves out or no longer qualifies has to tell the assessor within 30 days. Missing that notice can mean recalculation as nonhomestead and a penalty equal to 100 percent of the homestead benefit.

How do I dispute a Hubbard County valuation?

Talk to the assessor at 218-732-3552 first. Minnesota Statutes 274.01 then gives two stages. The local board of appeal and equalization, which is the town board or city council unless it has handed the job to the county, meets between April 1 and May 31 with at least ten days of published notice. It must finish within 20 days of convening, and its reductions cannot lower the assessor's total by more than one percent.

An owner who skips the local board, after being notified, generally cannot appear before the county board, so missing the spring meeting costs you a step. A late disagreement goes to the county board of equalization, where the auditor serves. Tax Court is the last stop, and a district court petition for a given tax year must be filed by April 30 of that year under Statutes 278.01.

What Hubbard County dates fall in the next few weeks?

  • November 15: the last day to pay the second half on qualifying agricultural property without penalty.
  • December: late penalty on unpaid halves keeps growing by 1 percent each month until it reaches the cap for the property type.
  • December 31, 2026: the final day to apply for homestead on a home you owned and lived in during the year.
  • April 30, 2027: the court filing date for a petition about taxes payable in 2027, which follows the March valuation notice.

A seller who closes before December 31 should tell the buyer about the homestead deadline, because the buyer's own application is what carries the benefit into 2027 taxes. The assessor at 218-732-3552 can mail or email the form.

What does a seller need to settle on a Hubbard County sale?

Pay any delinquent tax before recording. Hubbard's recorder asks for this in its recording guidance, and Minnesota Statutes 272.12 stops the auditor from transferring a parcel with delinquent tax on it. Current-year tax is not required at the time of recording unless the parcel is being split, and it is usually collected and paid through the closing settlement. Tax payments are not part of the electronic recording process, so the title company handles the payoff separately.

The recorder accepts abstract and Torrens documents through four trusted submitters: ePN, Indecomm Global Services, Corporation Service Company and Simplifile. State deed tax and mortgage registration tax are collected together with the recording fee. A deed uses an eCRV and, when needed, an electronic well disclosure certificate. For a payoff figure on the current year, ask the Hubbard County Treasurer's Office. Ask the assessor how a lake home is classified, since that decides which penalty rates and homestead rules apply.

More questions about Hubbard County, MN Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay Hubbard County property tax?

Payments go to the Auditor/Treasurer at the Government Center in Park Rapids, or through the Pay Your Taxes Online link on the county's I want to Pay page. Mail must be postmarked by the due date.

Does a Hubbard County cabin qualify for homestead?

Only if you own it and live in it as your primary home, or a qualifying relative does. Seasonal residential recreational property is a separate class, and a relative homestead is barred for any property that has been classified that way under the current owner.

When must I apply for Hubbard County homestead?

By December 31, 2026 for the current assessment, which affects taxes payable in 2027. You must own and occupy the property by that date, and applications can be made online, in person or by mail.

Are Hubbard County property taxes paid at closing?

Current-year tax is not required at recording unless the parcel is being split, but it is often settled at closing. Delinquent tax must be paid before the deed is recorded.

What is the Hubbard County assessor's phone number?

218-732-3552, at Property Records, 301 Court Ave., Park Rapids, MN 56470. The office handles valuation, classification, homestead and recording.

Who to contact in Lyon County

What we confirmed on official pages

What we could not confirm

What does the Lyon County Assessor do?

The Lyon County Assessor's Office sets the market value and classification of each parcel as of January 2 each year. It is at 607 West Main Street, Marshall, MN 56258.

Minnesota statutes require the assessor to inspect every property at least once in a five-year interval, and the county describes a quintile review that relies on a physical, in-person inspection to gather property characteristics. Valuation notices go out each spring, and local, county and state boards of equalization meet every year as a forum to appeal value or classification. The office also runs the Green Acres, blind or disabled homestead and local option disaster abatement programs, and takes homestead applications.

What does the Lyon County Auditor/Treasurer handle?

The Auditor/Treasurer is the county's chief financial officer and its property tax administrator, and also its chief election official. For taxes, that means calculating each bill, collecting current and delinquent real estate tax, managing escrow, settling receipts with the taxing entities, running forfeited land proceedings and handling special assessments including ditches.

By statute the Auditor/Treasurer is also a member of the County Board of Equalization. The county's online tools let you find and pay your property tax online and search property records, valuation, classification and sales information. If your parcel has ditch assessments, ask this office to itemize them.

What kind of county is Lyon County for a seller?

Lyon County has Marshall as its seat and makes up the Marshall Micropolitan Statistical Area. It covers 715 square miles of land, second only to Itasca among the four counties in this series.

The Yellow Medicine, Redwood and Cottonwood rivers cross the county on their way northeast, and the land is low rolling hills. The state legislature established the county in 1868 and 1869, naming it for Army officer Nathaniel Lyon, who was killed in the Civil War in 1861. In 1873 the western 43% became Lincoln County. Cities are Balaton, Cottonwood, Florence, Garvin, Ghent, Lynd, Marshall, Minneota, Russell, Taunton and Tracy.

The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 25,684 people, only 0.6% above 2020. Lyon is the most renter-heavy of the four counties: the owner-occupied rate is 72.5% for 2020 to 2024, and the 2020 census counted 33.6% of occupied units as renter-occupied.

  • Housing units in July 2025: 11,437, with just 23 building permits in 2025.
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $200,700, the lowest of the four.
  • Median gross rent: $781; median household income: $75,303.
  • Mean commute: 14.6 minutes, the shortest of the four.

What do the 2020 census and QuickFacts say about Lyon County homes and jobs?

Lyon County is more urban than the other three counties here: 53.5% of residents lived in urban areas in 2020, and the median age was 37.5. The county had 10,137 households in 11,180 housing units, with 9.3% vacant and a rental vacancy rate of 12.5%.

Census QuickFacts lists 12,732 people employed at employer establishments in 2023 across 814 establishments, and 2022 retail sales of $650.65 million, or $25,583 per resident, the highest per-person figure of the four counties. Bachelor's degree attainment is 31.1%, foreign-born residents make up 6.1%, and 11.2% of people age 5 and older speak a language other than English at home.

  • Two airports serve the county: Southwest Minnesota Regional Airport (MML) and Tracy Municipal Airport (TKC).
  • Camden State Park and Garvin State Park are inside the county, along with several state wildlife management areas.
  • The median home value of $200,700 is lower than in Isanti ($306,200) or Le Sueur ($316,500), and median gross rent is $781 a month.

When are Lyon County property taxes due?

Minnesota sets the schedule for Lyon County like every other county: half before May 16 and half before October 16 when a bill is over $100. Smaller bills are paid once, at the first-half date.

Lyon County tax dates and penalty rules from Minnesota law
ItemRule
First halfBefore May 16
Second halfBefore October 16
Qualifying seasonal commercial propertyFirst half before June 1, with an affidavit
Agricultural second halfNo penalty if paid by November 15
Late penalty cap8% homestead, 12% nonhomestead

Source: Minnesota Statutes section 279.01. One more point: the treasurer may accept a payment larger or smaller than the exact installment, and it goes first to the oldest installment still owed and to accrued penalty before tax when it falls short. A homestead owner in the National Guard or a reserve component on federal active service gets a four-month grace period with no penalty, and must send a copy of orders or form DD214 with the payment.

How do homestead applications work in Lyon County?

Fill out the homestead application online and print it, or print a blank and fill it out by hand. Return it by mail to the Lyon County Assessor's Office, 607 West Main Street, Marshall, MN 56258, or put it in the drop box at the rear entrance of the Lyon County Government Center.

One local exception: if the property is inside the City of Marshall, call 507-537-6771 to file for homestead. The county says homestead is the program it is asked about most often, and it has a plain-language FAQ on what a homestead is and why it matters. Classification matters most when a payment is late, because the penalty on a nonhomestead parcel starts at 4% instead of 2%.

The state's Homestead Credit Refund is a separate benefit from the Department of Revenue. Its due date is August 15 and it can be filed for up to one year after that date.

How can I appeal a Lyon County valuation?

Read the spring notice, call the assessor with your evidence, and then use the local, county or state board of equalization meetings the office describes if you still disagree. The Assessor's FAQ page lists each step, including what evidence to bring to the board.

If you take the matter to court, Minnesota Statutes section 278.01 says a petition must be served on the county auditor and filed with the district court administrator by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. A Tax Court appeal can begin after the valuation notice arrives and has to begin before May 1. The statute also gives an owner 60 days from the notice mailing date when a change in value or class is not announced until after February 28.

What should a Lyon County seller check before closing?

Ask the Auditor/Treasurer for the amount owed on your parcel, including penalty and any ditch or other special assessment, and compare it with your closing date. Ask the Assessor whether the homestead classification still matches how the house is used.

The Assessor's online property search shows the property record card, valuation, classification and characteristics for a parcel, and a separate tax information page shows statements and sales. Print the record card before you list, so the numbers you quote match the county's.

More questions about Lyon County, MN Property Tax Guide

Where do I mail a Lyon County homestead application?

Lyon County Assessor's Office, 607 West Main Street, Marshall, MN 56258. There is also a drop box at the rear entrance of the Lyon County Government Center.

Who do I call to file homestead for a house inside Marshall?

Call 507-537-6771. The county says properties within the City of Marshall file through that number.

How often does the Lyon County assessor inspect a property?

At least once in a five-year interval, under Minnesota law. The county uses a quintile review that includes an on-site, in-person inspection.

What is the court deadline to challenge a Lyon County tax?

April 30 of the year the tax is payable for a district court petition. A Tax Court appeal must start before May 1, under Minnesota Statutes section 278.01.

What is the largest late penalty on a Lyon County rental?

12% of the unpaid tax, which is the cap for nonhomestead property under Minnesota Statutes section 279.01. Homestead property is capped at 8%.

Cash Home Buyers in Minnesota
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Morrison County, MN Property Tax Guide sale

We buy Morrison County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Who to contact in Morrison County

Tax rate

Selling in Morrison County?
We buy Morrison County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What we could not confirm

What is Morrison County like for someone selling a house?

Morrison County is a mostly rural, river-and-lake county in central Minnesota, and Little Falls anchors it as seat of government and biggest town. Benton County gave up its northern strip to form it on February 25, 1856. The Mississippi River runs south through the western part, and Camp Ripley Military Reservation fills a big piece of the north-central area. Cass, Crow Wing, Mille Lacs, Benton, Stearns and Todd counties surround it.

The QuickFacts table for Morrison County, the July 2025 population estimate is 34,620, with 16,659 housing units across about 1,125 square miles of land. Owners live in 80.6 percent of occupied homes. For 2020 to 2024 the middle owner-occupied home value was $248,500, middle gross rent was $788 a month, and the median household earned $69,446.

The county's school district list includes Little Falls, Pierz, Royalton and Staples-Motley, plus Swanville, Upsala, Holdingford and others. A buyer comparing a house in Little Falls with one near Pierz is also comparing school districts.

What does the local economy mean for a Morrison County house?

The county's economy is spread thin across small employers. The Census Bureau counted 933 employer establishments and 8,532 jobs there in 2023, and workers spend a mean 28.6 minutes getting to work. About 23.4 percent of residents are 65 or older, and 92 percent of people lived in the same house a year earlier. The county issued 156 building permits in 2025.

Little Falls grew up around water power. A dam and sawmill built there in 1849 supplied the construction of Fort Ripley, and a third dam in 1887 drew in more industry. Pine Tree Lumber Company began its Little Falls operations in 1890, and Hennepin Paper Company started the same year. Charles A. Lindbergh State Park sits inside the county, along with part of Crow Wing State Park.

Sellers can ask the Assessor's Office what classification the parcel carries before listing. The county's appeals page names classification, along with estimated market value, as something an owner may contest.

Which offices in Little Falls deal with property tax and deeds?

All three offices share the Government Center at 213 1st Avenue SE, Little Falls, MN 56345. The county switchboard is 320-632-2941, with a toll-free line at 1-866-401-1111, and the front-line county offices post weekday hours from 8 to 4:30.

  • Auditor/Treasurer: sends the tax bills, collects the money and holds the payment counter. Details are on the county's property tax page.
  • Assessor's Office (Land Services): sets estimated market value and classification, and answers value questions at 320-632-0170.
  • Recorder: files deeds and other real estate papers, phone 320-632-0146. Its web page tells visitors the staff cannot advise on law or draft documents, and refers transfer questions to a real estate attorney or an abstract or title firm.

Online, the county directs people to Beacon for maps and tax statements, and to Landshark for recorded documents.

What are the Morrison County tax payment deadlines?

Two installments make up the real property bill, with deadlines of May 15 and then October 15, and extra dates for resorts, manufactured homes and farmland. Personal property and severed mineral interest taxes fall due alongside the real property installments. The county adds that a deadline falling on a weekend or legal holiday shifts to the next day the office is open.

Due dates on the Morrison County tax payment page
DateWhat is due
May 15Real property, first installment, or the entire bill if it totals $100 or under
May 31Resort property, first half
August 31Manufactured homes, first installment, or the entire bill if it totals $50 or under
October 15Non-agricultural real property, second half
November 15Agricultural real property and manufactured homes, second half

The statewide rule in Minn. Stat. 279.01 uses the same May and October split for bills above $100, and lets agricultural homestead and a few related classes pay the second half through November 15 without penalty.

What payment methods does the Morrison County treasurer accept?

The county lists six channels:

  • Counter: cash or a check made out to Morrison County Auditor/Treasurer, during office hours.
  • Drop box: at Broadway (Highway 27) and 2nd Street SE, emptied every day.
  • Postal mail: addressed to the Auditor/Treasurer at the Government Center. The county treats the postmark as proof of timely mailing.
  • Direct Debit: an enrollment form the county needs 30 days ahead of a due date.
  • Card or eCheck online: American Express, Discover, MasterCard and Visa.
  • Phone: 888-272-9829, then jurisdiction code 3314. Press 1 for personal property, 2 for real estate or 3 for mobile homes.

Fees on electronic payments are 2.59 percent for credit cards, 2.59 percent for debit cards with a $1.10 floor, and $2.15 for an eCheck.

What does a late tax payment cost in Morrison County?

An installment left unpaid at its deadline picks up 2 percent on a homestead and 4 percent on any other property. Section 279.01 repeats that charge when the balance is still open as the next month begins. After that, 1 percent more accrues each month through December. The ceiling is 8 percent for homestead property and 12 percent for everything else.

One break applies to mailed payments. The treasurer has to forgive the penalty if the envelope was postmarked by the Postal Service no more than one business day after the deadline, and only one time per owner. If the postmark is missing or smudged, a signed affidavit from the owner can establish the mailing date. The county board can also let the treasurer waive a penalty that would be unjust and unreasonable, so ask the Auditor/Treasurer whether Morrison County has adopted that policy.

What can you do if your Morrison County valuation looks too high?

Gather evidence and talk to the assessor before any hearing. The county's appeals page says the appeal concerns the current estimated market value or classification, which drives next year's taxes. Its advice is to bring recent comparable sales.

  1. Collect comparable recent sales.
  2. Phone the Assessor's Office at 320-632-0170 and go over your numbers with a county appraiser.
  3. If that fails, book a slot with your local appeal board, which sits in April.
  4. Still unhappy? Book the special appeal board, which sits in June. It will only hear you after the local board has.
  5. The final route is Minnesota Tax Court.

Hearing dates appear on the valuation notice and in local papers. This year's April and June sessions are over, and the next ones follow the same pattern. A dispute over last year's value cannot go to the assessor. It goes to Tax Court only, and must be filed in Tax Court by the end of April of the year the bill comes due.

Does a sale of a Morrison County house change the tax picture?

It does in two ways: the deed has to clear a tax check, and the homestead status resets. Before a deed is accepted for recording, Minn. Stat. 272.12 sends it past the auditor, who searches for unpaid delinquent tax and marks the deed. A recorder cannot take a deed without that mark.

A price above $3,000 also calls for a certificate of value, which section 272.115 has the buyer or seller hand to the auditor. The assessor then takes homestead status off the parcel for the following assessment year, unless the new owner applies and qualifies. With no application on file by December 31, the parcel is treated as nonhomestead that year.

Owing back tax, or holding an inherited or as-is property, is a reason to phone the Auditor/Treasurer for a payoff figure with penalties included. Ask whoever runs your closing how this year's bill will be split.

More questions about Morrison County, MN Property Tax Guide

Which number reaches the Morrison County assessor?

The assessor's line is 320-632-0170. For payments and balances, use the Government Center switchboard at 320-632-2941 and ask for the Auditor/Treasurer.

When does the last Morrison County installment fall due?

October 15 closes out non-agricultural real property. Farmland and manufactured homes run to November 15, which is a Sunday this year, so the effective date is Monday, November 16.

Can I use a credit card on my Morrison County tax bill?

Yes. Use the county's online payment link or call 888-272-9829 and enter jurisdiction code 3314. Expect a 2.59 percent convenience charge on a credit card.

What is the order of Morrison County appeal steps?

Take it to the assessor first, then the April local board, then the June special board, and finally Minnesota Tax Court. The special board hears only people who already went to the local board.

What does the Census report as a typical home value here?

$248,500, for the 2020 to 2024 period. That middle value covers the entire county, so a given house may differ a lot from that middle point.

Who to contact in Pope County

What we confirmed on official pages

  • Assessor 320-634-7715; appeal at spring valuation notice; assessor must be allowed to inspect property interior for board adjustment (MS 274.01)
  • 130 E. Minnesota Ave, Glenwood MN 56334; (320) 634-7700; Mon-Fri 8:00-4:30; second half real property taxes event page (from the county site listing; confirm with the office)

Where do I take property tax questions in Pope County?

Both property tax offices sit in the courthouse at 130 E. Minnesota Avenue in Glenwood. The Assessor, at 320-634-7715, sets the estimated market value and the class of each parcel. The Auditor/Treasurer, at 320-634-7706, prepares and mails the statements, takes payments and manages delinquent accounts. The Auditor/Treasurer's page puts the yearly mailing at more than 13,500 real estate and mobile home statements and the amount collected at over $14,000,000.

The Auditor/Treasurer is an elected post, and the office keeps weekday hours from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The same counter handles a change of taxpayer name or address, an ACH form for twice-a-year automatic withdrawal, and the sale of tax-forfeited land.

Sellers usually need both offices. The Assessor explains a value or a homestead question, and the Auditor/Treasurer supplies the balance that must be cleared before a deed can move.

What is Pope County like for someone selling a house?

Pope County is farm and lake country in west central Minnesota. It covers 717 square miles, with 670 of land and 47 of water, and its terrain is low rolling hills dotted with ponds. The Chippewa River runs through the western side, and Lake Minnewaska, Lake Emily and Lake Johanna are among the better-known waters. Glacial Lakes State Park is among the protected areas.

Glenwood is the county seat and largest city. Starbuck, Villard, Lowry, Cyrus, Farwell, Long Beach, Sedan, Westport and part of Brooten complete the list of cities. The county was identified by the legislature in 1862, named for General John Pope, and organized in 1866. Its 1930 Beaux-Arts courthouse is on the National Register of Historic Places.

From Census Bureau QuickFacts:

  • 11,420 residents on July 1, 2025, a 1.0% gain since 2020
  • 6,549 housing units, with 83.5% occupied by owners
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home of $255,100 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median household income of $76,220 and a 22.7 minute average drive to work
  • Only 33 building permits in 2025, and 27.5% of residents aged 65 or older

With few new homes being built, resale sellers here are often handling a parent's house or a lake property with an older owner.

What is happening with the Pope County 2027 levy?

On September 15, 2026 the County Board set a preliminary 2027 levy of $11,809,106, which is 3.4% above the 2026 levy of $11,420,799. State law lets the county hold or lower that figure at final adoption but not raise it. The county notes that its levy has averaged a 2.2% yearly increase since 2017, with a low of a 3.0% cut in 2021 and a high of a 6.9% rise in 2024.

The Truth-in-Taxation hearing is scheduled for Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 6:00 p.m. at the courthouse, so it is still ahead. Each parcel gets a single proposed-tax notice from the Auditor/Treasurer, but the county reminds owners that it decides only the county line. City, township, school and special district proposals have their own hearings, and those dates are printed on the notice. The 2027 budget also includes a one-time $1,950,000 draw from road and bridge fund balance.

How do I appeal a Pope County valuation?

The county tells owners that spring is the moment to act, when the valuation notice arrives with the tax statement. By the time proposed taxes come out in the fall it is too late. The usual route has these stops:

  • Call the Assessor at 320-634-7715 and discuss the value or class informally. The county's tax timeline says informal appeals run until the special County Board meeting in early June.
  • Go to your local board of appeal and equalization. Local meetings are by appointment through the Assessor. In 2026, for example, the Glenwood open book session ran at the Assessor's Office at 9:00 a.m. on April 20, and Rolling Forks Township met at its town hall on April 22.
  • Appear before the County Board of Appeal and Equalization. In 2026 it met at 6:30 p.m. on June 15 in the courthouse board room, and speakers needed an appointment made by June 10.

The county's appeals FAQ adds a warning that state law puts the burden of proof on the owner. Your evidence has to be strong enough to show the Assessor's number is wrong, and only relevant testimony given at the board counts.

When are Pope County property taxes due and what do late payments cost?

Real estate tax is paid in halves, with the first due May 15 and the second due October 15. The second half on class 2a agricultural land is not due until November 15. Pope County does not mail second-half statements, so the stub from the spring mailing is what you send back in the fall. Taxes of $100 or less must be paid in full with the first half.

The county's 2026 statement lists the penalty ladder for homestead and cabin property:

Pope County 2026 late penalties on homestead and cabin property, from the tax statement
Paid afterFirst half unpaidSecond half unpaid
May 162%not yet due
June 14%not yet due
July 15%not yet due
August 16%not yet due
September 17%not yet due
October 18%not yet due
October 168%2%
November 18%4%
December 18%5%

Nonhomestead land carries double the early rates, starting at 4% after May 15. The statement also says the office cannot accept post-dated checks, that a postmark from the Postal Service proves timely mailing, and that a private meter postmark does not.

What else shows up on a Pope County tax statement?

Bills here include a solid waste fee. The 2026 payable-year fee was $139 on any property with a building value of $5,000 or more, collected for the Pope/Douglas Solid Waste Management system at 320-763-9340. It is a charge listed apart from the value-based tax.

The homestead exclusion works as a reduction of taxable value. On the 2026 statement it peaks at $38,000 for a home valued at $95,000, shrinks by nine percent of the value above that, and disappears at $517,200. Special assessments for streets, sidewalks and sewers appear in their own section, and the county notes they are based on benefit to the property, not market value.

Many bills are paid through a lender's escrow account. The county mails the owner a copy anyway and sends the lender its own listing.

What tax relief can a Pope County owner use, and what happens when the house sells?

The statement describes two state refunds for homesteads owned and occupied on January 2. The regular refund applies when taxes exceed income-based thresholds and household income is under $142,490. The special refund applies when net tax on the homestead rose more than 12% and the increase was at least $100. Both use Form M1PR, due August 15. A senior deferral is also offered for owners 65 or older with household income of $96,000 or less who have lived in the home five years; the filing date for 2027 was November 1, 2026, so a new applicant would look at next year.

Sellers should ask the Auditor/Treasurer for a payoff before listing. If the property is a mobile home, the county's ownership-change form requires the entire parcel's taxes to be paid, and both the Auditor/Treasurer and the Assessor must sign before the Department of Motor Vehicles can transfer the title.

More questions about Pope County, MN Property Tax Guide

What number do I call to dispute a Pope County property value?

The Assessor's Office at 320-634-7715. Call before the early June special board meeting for an informal review, and make an appointment if you plan to speak at the County Board of Appeal and Equalization.

Does Pope County mail a bill for the second half?

No. The Auditor/Treasurer states that second-half statements are not mailed. Use the second-half stub from the statement you received in the spring, and mail it or bring it in by October 15.

What is the Pope County solid waste fee?

It is a charge on properties with a building value of $5,000 or more that supports the Pope/Douglas Solid Waste Management system. It was $139 for the 2026 taxes payable year. Call 320-763-9340 with questions about the fee.

Is the Pope County Truth-in-Taxation hearing coming up?

Yes. The county hearing is Thursday, December 3, 2026 at 6:00 p.m. at the courthouse in Glenwood. Other taxing bodies hold separate hearings listed on your proposed notice.

Can I pay Pope County property tax automatically?

Yes, through the ACH Real Estate Tax Payment Form on the Auditor/Treasurer's page. It deducts payments from a checking or savings account twice a year. Return the completed form to the office.

  • Wabasha County, MN Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Wabasha County, MN Property Tax Guide sale

Selling in Wabasha County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Wabasha County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.
